text:
Archbishop of Canterbury Presents Interfaith Award to Muslim Cleric Who Praised bin Laden
by @JamesMacpherson [COMMENTARY]

Editor’s note: Since this article was written, the Archbishop of Canterbury, after public outcry, has rescinded the interfaith award given to Hafiz Ashrafi on the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 attacks.

~~~

You can’t reconcile with people by ignoring what they actually say.

The Church of England last week gave a prestigious award to a senior Islamic leader.

Who cares, you say.

Well, you should care, because this story illustrates what I consider to be the incredible naivety of Western elites.

The Archbishop of Canterbury presented Hafiz Ashrafi with an award for Reconciliation and Interfaith Cooperation.

It’s a special award for people who do outstanding work building bridges between people of different faiths.

Ashrafi is the chairman of the Pakistan Ulema Council — a group of high-ranking Islamic scholars.

Here’s a photo of the presentation.

You can see there the Archbishop presenting the Reconciliation and Interfaith Cooperation Award to the winner.

And in case you don’t recognise her, that’s his wife in the middle.

Why would the Church of England give one of Pakistan’s most eminent Islamic scholars such an award?

Was it because in 2007, as reported in The Guardian, he…

“ … had decided to honour Osama bin Laden. He is to be given the title of Saifullah, or Sword of God.”

Or perhaps Ashrafi was given the reconciliation award because in 2013 he was reported as saying that…

“ … suicide attacks in Afghanistan are lawful because NATO troops are invaders that have occupied the country.”

Ashrafi later said he had been taken out of context, claiming that suicide bombings were un-Islamic but that he could understand why Afghans were fighting back.

Or maybe Ashrafi was given the award for interfaith reconciliation out of deep appreciation for his support, in 2014…

“… of Islamic blasphemy laws that condemn people to death if they insult Muhammad or disrespect the Koran.”

Afterall, nothing says I’m a leader when it comes to co-operating with other faiths than… if you disrespect us, you’ll be put to death.

Can you see why I’m struggling to understand how it is that the Archbishop of Canterbury is giving this man a prize… rather than a very wide berth?

I wonder what Hafiz Ashrafi thought of the archbishop as she handed him the award.

Afterall, the man she chose to honour said, in 2021, that women should not be shown in advertisements.

He expressed disbelief that…

“ … despite having so many good-looking men in the country, advertisers still hire women to represent their brands.”

In 2021 he also backed the then Pakistan Prime Minister’s assertion that women should wear the hijab in order to protect themselves from being raped by men who were unfairly impacted by women wearing few clothes.

I could go on and on with this stuff.

But I’ll give you just one more.

In April this year Hafiz Ashrafi told journalists that the war on Iran was not about stopping the Islamic Republic’s nuclear weapons program.

No, no. It was, instead, a plot hatched by Jews and Christians…

“… who wanted only to deprive the Iranian people of nuclear power.”

So here’s the Church of England bestowing an interfaith co-operation award on a man who blames “Jews and Christians” for what’s happening in Iran.

To add insult to injury, this award was presented on September 11.

There’s something almost breathtaking about the naivety of our public institutions.

And I think the problem is this… we keep assuming everyone wants what we want.

And we keep imagining that every culture is our culture, just with different food.

We convince ourselves that if we just offer the right award, use the right language, or bend over a little bit more, everyone will share our assumptions about liberty, equality and human dignity.

Except history proves they won’t.

And the refusal to understand that is not merely embarrassing. Sometimes it’s downright dangerous.

Because you can’t build genuine reconciliation by pretending profound differences don’t exist.

You can’t defend liberal values by assuming everyone shares them.

And you certainly can’t preserve a civilisation by congratulating people for occasionally agreeing with you while ignoring everything they have said when they don’t.

The West has spent years congratulating itself for being tolerant.

Perhaps it is time we became a little more discerning about what, exactly, we are tolerating. While we still have the chance.

While the Archbishop of Canterbury was handing out peace awards to an Islamic scholar who has praised Osama bin Laden and supported Pakistan’s blasphemy laws…

The Church of England in Leeds was putting on display a tapestry paying tribute to those killed in Gaza — including, it appears, members of Palestinian Islamic Jihad and Hamas.

Both of which, I should add, are banned terrorist groups in the UK.

Church officials said they weren’t aware that terrorists were among those named in the tapestry, which was being displayed as…

“… an act of remembrance, honouring their lives and the immense loss to humanity”.

An admirable sentiment.

Although apparently one with some interesting exclusions.

Because the tapestry does NOT include the names of Israelis murdered when Hamas invaded Israel on October 7.

Church Rector Paul Maybury was asked why dead Jews were not recognised.

For instance… what about the Bibas children — two little Jewish boys kidnapped by Hamas terrorists on October 7 and subsequently murdered?

A reporter asked the Rector…

“So, what’s your view on kidnapping the Bibas children, and murdering them with their bare hands after kidnapping and torturing them?”

After a long pause, the Rector replied…

“I understand that the history is complex.”

After being pressed to condemn the murder of two little Jewish boys, the church leader finally conceded this…

“I condemn all killing.”

So the deaths of Palestinians — including terrorists — are honoured specifically.

But the deaths of Jews — even two little boys — are not treated with any humanity, only with generalities.

The perverse part is that on the tapestry being displayed in the Leeds Church… the names of the murdered little boys are not recorded.

But the names of the terrorists who kidnapped and murdered those little boys may well be listed on the honour roll.

The “Free Palestine” mind virus is incredible. It even makes church leaders destroy their own moral compass and embrace Islamist killers.

Or maybe that’s just what happens to a church that decides they no longer believe their own message.

They start scratching about for a cause to ally with in the absence of their own members — most of whom fled long ago.

Read the full piece at https://t.co/uYKoJ8a9WF

He then told me he wasn't going to interview someone who didn't take interviews seriously and told me to leave.

I told him I just walked three miles, had no transportation, and if he gave me some time to freshen up in the restroom I would appreciate the opportunity to interview.

He didn't acknowledge my request and asked politely that I leave. So, I left. I walked three miles back home.

I was in need of some money, I was absolutely devastated. I felt like such a fuck up and a loser.

In retrospect, fuck that guy. I was just a kid man. God damn, at least give a muthafucker a chance to shoot their shot.

text:
My name is William Hudson.

Over the years, I’ve developed one habit when looking at the market:

I don’t start by asking, “Which stock is going up?” I start by asking, “What kind of market are we in?”

Because what determines the quality of a trade usually isn’t the company name.

It’s what’s happening underneath the surface:

Interest rates, capital flows, market sentiment, and the amount of risk you’re taking at your entry price.

Right now, I see the U.S. market as a classic case of divergence.

On one side, AI, semiconductors, and high-growth tech stocks remain strong.

On the other, Treasury yields are back near elevated levels, energy prices remain high, and macro pressure is building.

That tells me opportunities are still out there.

But the way money is being made is changing.

Before, you could chase momentum. Now, it makes more sense to wait for price.

So I’m not broadly bearish, and I’m not blindly chasing the upside either.

My strategy comes down to one sentence:

Keep tracking the strongest sectors, but only step in when the risk/reward becomes attractive again.

Here are the 7 stocks I’m watching most closely right now:

$MSFT (Microsoft)

Latest close: $493.78

— Key watch zone: $487–$492

Microsoft remains one of the more resilient mega-cap tech names.

But in an environment where Treasury yields stay elevated, high-valuation tech stocks as a group are still sensitive to interest rates.

So near $500, I’m not chasing just because the AI story remains strong.

If MSFT pulls back toward $487–$492 and starts to stabilize, that’s when I’ll reassess.

$COST (Costco)

Latest close: $895.31

— Key watch zone: $880–$890

Costco reports earnings on September 24.

From a market perspective, the real question right now isn’t whether Costco is a great company.

It’s this:

Has the current valuation already priced in most of the good news?

That’s why I’d rather stay patient before earnings.

The market’s repricing after the report matters more to me than trying to predict the result beforehand.

$ARM (Arm Holdings)

Latest close: $275.61

— Not chasing short term

First watch zone:

$260–$265

Deeper pullback zone:

$250–$255

ARM gained 8.57% on September 17 and another 4.04% on September 18.

From a market perspective, that tells me risk appetite in semiconductors has clearly improved.

But it also tells me something else:

Short-term positioning is getting crowded.

I respect strong trends.

But a strong trend doesn’t mean every price is a good entry.

$RBRK (Rubrik)

Latest close: $106.71

— Waiting for sentiment to cool

First watch zone:

$100–$103

Second watch zone:

$95–$98

RBRK moved quickly from $86.65 on September 11 to above $106.

That kind of move tells me capital is chasing high-growth, high-beta software names.

But structurally, the bigger the short-term move,

the more sensitive the stock becomes to any negative headline.

So here, I’d rather wait than chase.

$TSLA (Tesla)

Latest close: $364.27

— Watching $355–$360

Second watch zone:

$348–$352

Tesla has recently traded mostly between $350 and $375.

That tells me the market still has strong event-driven expectations around the stock,

but capital hasn’t produced a true one-way breakout yet.

So what I care about most right now is:

After a pullback, does real buying support show up again?

I’m not interested in guessing whether the next candle is green or red.

$NVO (Novo Nordisk)

Latest close: $43.24

— Watching $41.50–$42.50

NVO has a completely different setup from the rest of this list.

Compared with AI and high-growth tech, short-term positioning here doesn’t look nearly as crowded.

In a high-rate, high-volatility market,

that can actually be worth paying attention to.

I’m not going to ignore a stock just because it isn’t exploding higher.

Sometimes:

The best opportunities come from areas of the market that everyone else is temporarily ignoring.

$HOOD (Robinhood)

Latest close: $119.82

— Not chasing here

First watch zone:

$110–$114

Second watch zone:

$103–$107

HOOD gained 9.12% on September 18.

From a market perspective, that wasn’t just a normal move.

It reflected renewed risk appetite around high-beta fintech names and expectations for stronger trading activity.

But stocks like this have one clear characteristic:

When risk appetite rises, they move fast. When risk appetite fades, they can pull back just as fast.

So near $120, I’m not chasing.

I’d rather wait for the market to offer me a better risk/reward setup.

Over the next week, I’m not just watching these 7 stocks.

I’m watching four bigger things:

First, can Treasury yields stabilize?

If the 10-year yield stays near 5%, high-valuation tech stocks could remain under pressure.

Second, can oil prices come down?

If crude stays above $100 for an extended period, it keeps pressure on inflation and interest rates.

Third, will AI and semiconductor strength continue to broaden out?

If only a handful of stocks are moving higher while the rest of tech fails to participate, I’ll become more cautious.

Fourth, U.S.-China negotiations around AI, trade, and critical minerals.

Those developments could directly affect sentiment across semiconductors, AI, and related supply chains.

So right now, I’m not asking:

“Which stock is guaranteed to go up next week?”

I’m asking:

“If volatility hits, which stocks could move into a price range where the risk is finally worth taking?”

That’s how I’m looking at the market right now.

Read the market first, then pick the stock.

Control risk first, then think about returns.

Being bullish doesn’t mean chasing. Liking a company doesn’t mean abandoning price discipline.

Save this watchlist.

I’ll keep updating it as the market structure changes.

For personal market commentary only. Not financial advice.

text:
🙏💜 AN ANGEL ANSWERED MY PRAYERS! 💜🙏

I have been desperately trying to find someone to accompany me on my trip to Utah this Tuesday to see Dr. Jones at the Bateman Horne Center. With how sick I am, traveling alone simply isn't a safe option.

Unfortunately, my mom, sister, Barry, and regular caregiver have all been unable to make the trip with me, despite everyone trying to help.

I was honestly getting to the point where I thought I might just have to rough it and try to make the trip on my own.

But here's the thing about living with severe chronic illness…

My brain still thinks I can do things that my body keeps reminding me I can't. 💔

In my mind, I was telling myself I could just push through and make this trip alone if I absolutely had to.

But this morning, my heart rate was already 109 BPM just trying to stand up, accompanied by palpitations and significant shortness of breath. It was in that moment that the harsh reality of what my body can and cannot do hit me like a ton of bricks.

My mind may still believe I can push through and do the things I used to, but my body keeps reminding me that I simply can't.

If simply standing up is that much of a struggle, imagine trying to navigate airports, flights, luggage, a hotel, and medical appointments all on my own.

It's a heartbreaking reality when your mind wants so badly to be independent, but your body simply won't cooperate. I want to be able to do these things for myself, but the reality is that I need help, and trying to push through could leave me even sicker.

AND THEN AN ANGEL STEPPED IN! 🥹💜

Stacia Hood, a friend of my sister Lindsey, has offered to accompany me and help care for me throughout my trip, out of the kindness in her heart!

Someone who barely knows me is willing to take time out of her own life to travel with me, help me with my daily needs, and make sure I can get to this incredibly important appointment.

Stacia, I cannot even begin to express how grateful I am for you! You have lifted such an enormous weight off my shoulders. Your kindness and generosity mean more to me than you could possibly know.

You truly are an answer to my prayers! 💜

And a huge thank you to my sister Lindsey for connecting us and continuing to help me through all of this. I love you! 🥰

Stacia's incredibly generous offer means so much more than just having someone to travel with. She's making it possible for me to get the medical care I desperately need without having to attempt something my body simply cannot handle on its own.

If anyone is able to contribute toward the travel costs of this trip, even a few dollars would mean so much. Every donation helps make this trip possible!

💜 Ways to help:

GoFundMe: [https://t.co/c4fni5OvMT](https://t.co/c4fni5OvMT) 

GiveSendGo: [https://t.co/Ja7bTI2FNf](https://t.co/Ja7bTI2FNf)

If you're unable to donate, sharing this post would also mean the world to me!

Thank you to everyone who continues to support me, pray for me, and help me keep fighting for answers and treatment.

I am so incredibly grateful for people like Stacia, who remind me that even in the hardest moments, there are still incredibly kind people willing to step up and help.

Sometimes the greatest blessing isn't someone who can fix what you're going through, but someone who is willing to walk beside you through it. 🥹💜

text:
The English arrived in 1607 with a plan for the Powhatan. The Powhatan had a plan for them, and it was better.
Wahunsenacah ruled roughly thirty nations across the Virginia tidewater — tens of thousands of people, a capital, a tribute system, a foreign policy. He had watched Europeans come and go on this coast for decades. He knew what ships meant, and he knew what metal meant.
What he wanted from the English was specific: tools, weapons, and metalwork he could not otherwise get, and a client settlement close enough to trade with, weak enough to control, and dependent on him for food.
That last condition was the whole of the strategy. A colony that could feed itself was a rival. A colony that could not was an asset.
For the first three years it worked exactly as designed. The English chose a site nobody else wanted — marshy, brackish, defensible against Spanish ships and lethal to the men living on it. They failed to plant enough. They went looking for gold. And every winter they came to the Powhatan to trade for corn.
In the depths of the Starving Time, Wahunsenacah made them an offer: move 40 miles upriver, live under his protection, make tools and metalwork for him, and he would feed them.
He was not being generous. It was the arrangement he had wanted from the beginning, stated plainly at the moment they were least able to refuse it.

from "Desperate Shores," episodes 4 and 7

text:
In a major leap forward for regenerative medicine, independent research groups have developed functional, three-dimensional “mini pancreases” from living human stem cells. The engineered tissues can detect changes in glucose and release insulin without external control, raising the possibility of a biological treatment for insulin-dependent diabetes.

The implantable structures are designed to function inside the body and interact with a patient’s biological systems. In Type 1 diabetes, the immune system mistakenly destroys insulin-producing beta cells in the pancreatic islets. Current treatment relies heavily on artificial pancreas systems that pair continuous glucose monitors with external insulin pumps controlled by software.

The new approach seeks to replace that machinery with living tissue. Researchers use induced pluripotent stem cells, or iPSCs, to develop unspecialized cells into functional human islet organoids, then use tissue-engineering techniques to help them survive after implantation.

At the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, researchers developed an implantable device with an oxygen-generating system designed to keep encapsulated islet cells functioning. In preclinical tests, the system maintained cell function for at least 90 days. Researchers at the Wake Forest University School of Medicine separately used 3D printing to create supportive environments that kept human islets healthy and responsive to glucose.

Unlike traditional donor-cell transplants, which can require lifelong immunosuppressive drugs, the new implants use semipermeable, biocompatible membranes to protect the cells. Microscopic pores allow glucose and insulin to pass while blocking immune cells from attacking the tissue.

The technology is not yet available as a routine treatment and remains in preclinical development and early-stage research. Newer devices have maintained healthy blood sugar levels in animal studies for months.

Early human testing preparations are underway through international efforts, including the European Union’s VANGUARD Project, which has completed development of a retrievable, implantable bioartificial pancreas device. Researchers still need to establish the implants’ long-term durability, blood-vessel integration and safety in humans, meaning regulatory approval remains years away.

If human trials prove successful, the technology could eventually offer a regenerative way to restore insulin production and reduce reliance on lifelong diabetes management.

text:
Before inflation rates became everyday headlines, Filipinos had a much simpler way of understanding whether life was getting more expensive.

They looked at galunggong.

For decades, the humble round scad was more than the so-called “poor man’s fish.” Its retail price became an informal yardstick for the cost of living: if galunggong was getting expensive, ordinary families were probably feeling the squeeze.

The association became particularly prominent during the administration of President Corazon Aquino, when the price of galunggong figured heavily in public discussions about inflation and purchasing power.

It was easy to understand. Economists could talk about percentages and price indices, but almost everyone understood what it meant when a basic fish suddenly cost more.

Today, however, galunggong isn’t quite the economic thermometer it used to be.

WHY GALUNGGONG WORKED

A good informal price benchmark needs to be something ordinary consumers regularly buy.

Galunggong once fit that description perfectly.

It was widely available, relatively inexpensive and commonly eaten by working-class households. Watching its price rise therefore offered an immediate, relatable picture of how far a family’s money could go.

But the usefulness of that comparison depended on galunggong itself remaining an ordinary, affordable commodity.

That has changed.

WHEN THE YARDSTICK STARTED MOVING

In recent years, galunggong prices have reached as high as ₱400 per kilo in some markets—sometimes making the former “poor man’s fish” more expensive than chicken and certain cuts of pork.

More importantly, galunggong has its own complicated supply problems.

Round scad is predominantly wild-caught, making supply vulnerable to fishing conditions, declining catches and fuel costs. Government-imposed closed fishing seasons temporarily restrict catches in important fishing grounds so fish populations can reproduce.

Imports have also been used to augment domestic supply.

All these factors can cause galunggong prices to move for reasons that have little to do with the general direction of consumer prices.

A sudden increase could reflect inflation. But it could also reflect fewer fish being caught, a closed fishing season or a temporary supply shortage.

That makes galunggong a much less reliable shorthand for the overall cost of living.

THERE IS NO NEW ‘GALUNGGONG INDEX’

No single commodity has formally replaced it.

Today, inflation is measured through the Consumer Price Index or CPI compiled by the Philippine Statistics Authority. Instead of asking how much one fish costs, the CPI monitors price changes across a broad basket of goods and services households actually consume.

Food is only one part of it. Housing, electricity, gas, transportation and other expenses also matter.

Within food, rice remains particularly significant because of its importance to Filipino household spending. Its price movements can strongly affect food inflation, especially for lower-income families.

But rice alone isn’t inflation either.

That is precisely why economists use a basket rather than a single product.

FROM ECONOMIC YARDSTICK TO ECONOMIC STORY

Galunggong hasn’t lost its significance.

Its price can still tell us plenty about food security, fisheries, imports, fuel costs and the purchasing power of households trying to put protein on the table.

What has changed is what that price can reliably tell us.

Once, asking “Magkano na ang galunggong?” was almost a shorthand way of asking how expensive life had become.

Today, the answer may tell us as much about what is happening at sea as what is happening to prices everywhere else.

Galunggong remains an important Filipino economic symbol.

It just isn’t the yardstick it used to be.

(✍️: Top Dagohoy)

A LEWIS is a simple, but ingenious device employed by operative Masons to raise heavy blocks of stone into place. It consists of three metal parts: two wedge-shaped sidepieces, and a straight centerpiece, that fit together (tenon).

A dovetailed recess is cut into the top of the stone block (mortise). The two outer pieces are inserted first and then spread by the insertion of the centerpiece. The three parts are then bolted together, a metal ring or shackle is attached and the block is hoisted by hook, rope and pulley. By this means, the block is gripped securely. Once set in its place in the structure, the lewis is removed leaving the upper surface smooth with no clamp or chains on the outside to interfere with the laying of the next course of stones.

Our ancient operative brethren used this tool as early as the Roman era. Stones with the mortised cavity for the insertion of a lewis have been found in England in Hadrian’s Wall built c. 121-127 CE. Archaeologists have found further evidence of its use by the Saxons in England in buildings constructed in the 7th century. The origin of the term ‘lewis’ for this device is uncertain. Some authorities trace its etymology to the French levis from lever – to lift, hoist, raise; and louve – a sling, grip or claw for lifting stones.

Masonic historians conclude that the term came into use in the 18th century. The Lecture in the Second Degree published by William Preston in the 1780s contains a lengthy discourse on the Lewis.

WM- Brother J.W., How were the sons of craftsmen named?

JW – To the son on whom these honors were bequeathed, the appellation of Lewis was given, that from henceforth he might be entitled to all the privileges which that honor conferred, W. Sir.

There are many references to the Lewis in early Masonic Catechisms. The Wilkinson MS Catechism (c 1730 / 1740) states the following:

Q. What’s a Mason’s Sons Name?

A. Lewis

A paragraph in a version of the Junior Warden’s Lecture used in the United Grand Lodge of England dating from 1801 gives this instructive explanation: “The word Lewis denotes strength, and is here depicted by certain pieces of metal dovetailed into a stone, which forms a cramp, and enables the operative Mason to raise great weights to certain heights with little encumbrance, and to fix them in their proper places. Lewis, likewise denotes the son of a Mason; his duty is to bear the heat and burden of the day, from which his parents, by reason of their age, ought to be exempt; to help them in time of need, and thereby render the close of their days happy and comfortable; his privilege for so doing is to be made a Mason before any other person however dignified.”

These three names share a deep linguistic and historical connection, primarily originating in Ancient Mesopotamia, the Middle East, and the Caucasus.
Sargon
Origin & Etymology: The name is the Greek and biblical translation of the Akkadian regnal name Šarru-kīn. It combines šarru (Akkadian for "king") and kīnu (meaning "true," "established," or "legitimate").
Historical Significance: It is most famously associated with Sargon of Akkad (24th century BCE), the legendary founder of the Akkadian Empire. Later, the Neo-Assyrian ruler Sargon II (8th century BCE) adopted the throne name to establish the legitimacy of his rule.
Sargis
Origin & Etymology: The name is the Classical Syriac and Armenian form of the Latin name Sergius. It originates from the ancient Roman gens (clan) Sergia, which etymologists suspect may connect to the Latin verb servare ("to guard" or "to preserve").
Sako
Origin & Etymology: Sako operates on a few different historical tracks depending on the region:
In the Middle East: Among Assyrians and Armenians, Sako is a popular, affectionate diminutive (or pet form) of the proper name Sargis.
In the Balkans: In Albania, it functions as a standalone occupational surname for a "church servant" or as a nickname for the Muslim name Isak (Isaac).
In Asia: It is also an unrelated Japanese surname (written as 佐古) meaning "HELP" and "ancient".

The Foundation Stone (Hebrew: אֶבֶן הַשְּׁתִיָּה, romanized: ʾEḇen haŠeṯīyyā), or the Noble Rock (Arabic: الصخرة المشرفة, romanized: al-Saḵrah al-Mušarrafah), is the rock at the center of the Dome of the Rock in Jerusalem. It is also known as the Pierced Stone because it has a small hole on the southeastern corner that enters a cavern beneath the rock known as the Well of Souls.

Traditional Jewish sources mention the stone as the place from which the creation of the world began. Classical Jewish sources also identify its location with that of the Holy of Holies.[1][2]

Location
The rock is located towards the centre of the Temple Mount, at the top of Jerusalem's Old City southern hill. The current shape is the result of an expansion by Herod the Great on top of vaults over a summit called Mount Moriah which three millennia ago was the highest elevation in early Jerusalem's proximity to the City of David.[citation needed]

Early Muslim writings argue that the Dome of the Rock, completed in 691, is the site of the Holy of Holies and therefore the location of the Foundation Stone. The history by the 9th-century writer al-Tabari has Kaʿb al-Aḥbār, a Jewish convert to Islam, asking the caliph Umar to build a mosque over the rock, to which Umar responds, "O Ka'b, you are imitating the Jewish religion!" Al-Tabari then identifies the rock with the place where the Romans had "buried the temple (bayt al-maqdis) at the time of the sons of Israel."[3] Pirqe de-Rabbi Eliezer (9th century) also wrote: "Rabbi Ishmael said: In the future, the sons of Ishmael (the Arabs) will do fifteen things in the Land of Israel [...] They will fence in the breaches of the walls of the Temple and construct a building on the site of the sanctuary."[4]

Jewish sources have debated the precise location of the rock. Benjamin of Tudela wrote (c. 1170) that the site was in front of the Dome, on the site of the Western Wall.[5] The Travels of Petachia of Ratisbon,[6] c. 1180, and Travels of a Student of the Ramban[7] (c. 1400) state that "on the Temple Mount stands a beautiful sanctuary which an Arab king built long ago, over the place of the Temple sanctuary and courtyard." Obadiah Bartenura says in a 1488 letter from Jerusalem that "I sought the Foundation Stone [which marks] the former place of the Ark of the Covenant, and many told me that it is beneath a tall and beautiful dome which the Arabs built in the Temple, but the space beneath this dome is secured, such that no man may come to it, viz. to the place of the Foundation Stone, for the dome is very large."[8] David ben Solomon ibn Abi Zimra was convinced (c. 1570) that "under the dome [on the Temple Mount] – there is the Foundation Stone, undoubtedly – which the Arabs call al-Sakrah".[9]

Other sources, operating under the belief that the Southern Wall of the Temple Mount as it stood in their time was the Southern Wall of the Biblical era, argued that the measurements given in the Talmud do not reconcile.[10] The Holy of Holies ends up being too far north and they therefore locate the Foundation Stone as being directly opposite the current exposed section of the Western Wall, where no building currently stands. This is the view of Isaac Luria[11] and the Maharsha,[12] who state the prophecy that "Zion will become a ploughed field" indicates that no dwelling will be established there until the time of the Redemption. It therefore follows that the footprint of the Temple courtyard and Holy of Holies is situated in the unbuilt area between the Dome of the Rock and al-Aqsa Mosque.[13]

Some believe the position is north of the Dome of the Rock, opposite the Gate of Mercy, which Immanuel Hai Ricchi[14] identifies as the Shushan Gate mentioned in the Talmud. This gate was described as being opposite the opening of the sanctuary.[15]

Modern Jewish academics list four possible locations of the Foundation Stone:[16]

The stone that was located beneath the Ark of the Covenant is the one under the Dome of the Rock.[17]
The stone that was located beneath the altar is now the one that is under the Dome of the Rock.[18]
The stone that was located beneath the Ark of the Covenant is now near El Kas fountain to the South of the Dome of the Rock.[13]
The stone that was located beneath the Ark of the Covenant is now inside the Spirits Dome situated to the north of the Dome of the Rock.[15]

Description
Although the rock is part of the surrounding 90 million-year-old, Upper Turonian Stage, Late Cretaceous karsted limestone,[citation needed] the southern side forms a ledge, with a gap between it and the surrounding ground; a set of steps currently uses this gap to provide access from the Dome of the Rock to the Well of Souls beneath it.

Archaeologist Leen Ritmeyer reported that there are sections of the rock cut completely flat, which north-to-south have a width of 6 cubits,[19] precisely the width that the Mishnah credits to the wall of the Holy of Holies.[20] According to Ritmeyer, a rectangular rock-cutting he discovered on the Foundation Stone marks the location where the Ark of the Covenant stood within the Holy of Holies.[21] Ritmeyer's analysis was welcomed among biblical archeologists; however, scholars stated that this theory cannot be actually verified.[22]

The rock has several artificial cuts in its surface generally attributed to the Crusaders, whose frequent damage to the rock was so severe that the Christian kings of Jerusalem placed a protective marble slab over the rock. The marble slab was removed after Jerusalem had been taken over by Saladin in 1187.[citation needed]

Measuring the flat surface as the position of the southern wall of a square enclosure, the west and north sides of which are formed by the low clean-cut scarp at these edges of the rock, at the position of the hypothetical centre is a rectangular cut in the rock that is about 2.5 cubits (min. 120.4 cm SI) long and 1.5 cubits (min. 72.24 cm SI) wide, which are the dimensions of the Ark of the Covenant (according to the Book of Exodus).[23]

The Mishnah[24] gives the height of the rock as three thumb-breadths (min. 6 cm SI) above the ground. Radbaz[25] discusses the apparent contradiction of the Mishnah's measurements and the actual measurement of the rock within the Dome he estimates as a "height of two men" above the ground. He concluded that many changes in the natural configuration of the Temple Mount have taken place which can be attributed to excavations made by the various occupiers of Jerusalem since the Second Temple construction.

Jewish significance
Main article: Temple in Jerusalem
The Mishnah in tractate Yoma[26] mentions a stone situated in the Holy of Holies that was called Shetiya and had been revealed by the early prophets (i.e. David and Samuel).[27]

An early Christian source noting Jewish attachment to the rock may be found in the Itinerarium Burdigalense, written between 333 and 334 CE when Jerusalem was under Roman rule, which describes a "perforated stone to which the Jews come every year and anoint it, bewail themselves with groans, rend their garments, and so depart."[28]

According to the sages of the Talmud,[29] it was from this rock that the world was created, itself being the first part of the Earth to come into existence.[30] According to the Talmud, it was close to the Foundation Stone, on the site of the altar, that God gathered the earth that was formed into Adam. It was on this rock that Adam—and later Cain and Abel and Noah—offered sacrifices to God. Jewish sources identify this rock as the place of the Binding of Isaac mentioned in the Bible, where Abraham fulfilled God's test to see if he would be willing to sacrifice his son. The mountain is identified as Moriah in Genesis 22. It is also identified as the rock upon which Jacob dreamt about angels ascending and descending on a ladder and consequently consecrating and offering a sacrifice upon.[31]

The Roman-era midrash Tanhuma[1] sums up the centrality of and holiness of the site in Judaism:

As the navel is set in the centre of the human body,
so is the land of Israel the navel of the world...
situated in the centre of the world,
and Jerusalem in the centre of the land of Israel,
and the sanctuary in the centre of Jerusalem,
and the holy place in the centre of the sanctuary,
and the ark in the centre of the holy place,
and the Foundation Stone before the holy place,
because from it the world was founded.

When, according to the Bible, King David purchased a threshing floor owned by Araunah the Jebusite,[32] it is believed that it was upon this rock that he offered the sacrifice mentioned in the verse. He wanted to construct a permanent temple there, but as his hands were "bloodied", he was forbidden to do so himself. The task was left to his son Solomon, who completed the Temple in c. 950 BCE.

Toledot Yeshu reports that "It was called Shetiyya because God placed it there (שת אותה יה; cf. Zohar, Vayechi 43), and this is the stone which Jacob libated with wine. On it were written the letters of the Explicit Name, and anyone who knew them could perform magic to his heart's desire. The Sages feared lest youths obtain the Name and destroy the world, so they set two iron hounds at the gate, which would bark at any comer to cause him to forget what he had learned. In the words of the Zohar, "The world was not created until God took a stone called Even haShetiya and threw it into the depths where it was fixed from above till below, and from it the world expanded. It is the centre point of the world and on this spot stood the Holy of Holies."

Role in the Temple
Situated inside the Holy of Holies, the Foundation Stone is believed to have been the rock upon which the Ark of the Covenant was placed in Solomon's Temple.[33] During the Second Temple period when the Ark of the Covenant was not present, the stone was used by the High Priest who offered up the incense and sprinkled the blood of the sacrifices on it during the annual Yom Kippur service.

Commemoration in Jewish law
The Jerusalem Talmud states:

Women are accustomed not to prepare or attach warp threads to a weaving loom from Rosh Chodesh Av onwards (till after Tisha B'Av), because during the month of Av the Foundation Stone [and the Temple] was destroyed.[34]

Citing this, the Mishnah Berurah[35] rules that not only are women not to prepare or attach warp threads to a weaving loom, but it is forbidden for anyone to make, buy or wear new clothes or shoes from the beginning of the week in which Tisha B'Av falls until after the fast, and that people should ideally not do so from the beginning of Av. This period is known as The Nine Days.

In further commemoration of the Foundation Stone, it is also forbidden to eat meat or drink wine from the beginning of the week in which Tisha B'av falls until after the fast. Some have the custom to refrain from these foodstuffs from Rosh Chodesh Av, while others do so from the Seventeenth of Tammuz.[36]

Liturgical references
In the days when Selichot are recited, in the days leading up to Rosh Hashanah until Yom Kippur, the supplications include the following references:

טענתנו גפי קרת נתונים, ישבתנו שן סלע איתנים

Translation:
You carried us and placed us on the [Holy] City's height, You settled us on the Patriarch's rocky peak.[37]

רבוצה עליו אבן שתית חטובים ...שמה בתוך לפני מזיב מאשנבים

Translation:
Upon it lying the stone from which the foundation was hewn... Who gives ear from which the waters flow [i.e. the foundation stone "from which flow all the waters of the world"].[38]

During Sukkot, the following references to the Foundation Stone are mentioned in the Hoshanot recital:

הושענא! – אבן שתיה – הושענא

Translation:
Please save! – Foundation Stone – Please save!

הושענא! – תאדרנו באבן תלולה – הושענא

Translation:
Please save! – Adorn us with the elevated Stone – Please save!

A Conversation - Guru Nanga & Mango: Midterms & The Course of Honor (6/6)

MANGO: Numbers.

GURU NANGA: Forty-six per cent of Democrats say they are very enthusiastic about voting. Thirty-one per cent of Republicans. Rome measured enthusiasm in turnips. Cruder, but faster.

MANGO: The races.

GURU NANGA: North Carolina: Roy Cooper, a former governor, against Michael Whatley, a former party chairman who has never run for anything. Texas: James Talarico and Ken Paxton at 47 to 46. Ohio: Sherrod Brown, back again, against Jon Husted at 48 to 45. Maine: Susan Collins behind Troy Jackson, 45 to 48. Georgia: Mr Ossoff at 49 to 43 in a Republican pollster's survey.

MANGO: Prediction.

GURU NANGA: Rome's rule was that the emperor's party lost the midterm to the Praetorian Guard. Ours is gentler. The president's party loses seats and the losers write books.

MANGO: Was Caenis happy?

GURU NANGA: She died in the year 74, rich, in a villa on the Via Nomentana. When Vespasian's son Domitian saw her afterwards, she offered the customary kiss and he gave her his hand instead. Her freedman Aglaus and his children put up an altar and called her optuma patrona. The best boss. It is the only approval rating from that decade that survives. Unanimous.

MANGO: Sample size?

GURU NANGA: Four. Which is more than the House managed on Wednesday.

THE BILL

The bill came. Guru Nanga paid it. It did not smell.

MANGO: A finding.

GURU NANGA: Suetonius wrote half a sentence and a woman got a novel. Washington writes all day and a woman got a printer. The length of the record is not the honour. The rule is the honour. Rome had one and kept it badly. We have forms.

MANGO: And the bag?

GURU NANGA: The bag remains defenseless. We will walk home.

text:
If your startup is struggling to grow, it’s usually because you’re not focused on a specific kind of customer.

I’ve never met a founder who said their product or service wasn’t great so I’m assuming that’s the case so it comes done to focusing on an ICP.

Too often I hear, “oh our ICP is large enterprises.”

That will never work!

Even if you say your ICP is financial services, that isn’t super helpful either…

Look at this example:

If you were trying to close Citi Bank, and you offered a local small credit union in Ohio as the reference customer, do you think that’s a good reference customer?  Probably not, even though they are both “financial services.”

They buy different, have different needs etc.

Early on you need to focus, and for many startups that means a much much more narrow focus than what they are doing today.

That’s what helps your SDRs message land, your AEs actually close deals, and your channel partners know where to bring you in.

text:
Week 4, Day 3 The Kingdom of Eternal Dominion

The coast of Spain had offered hope.
The landing...Destroyed it.

The battered twin-engine aircraft screamed across the broken coastline, its damaged landing gear collapsing the moment it struck the ground. Sparks erupted beneath the fuselage as the aircraft skidded across fractured stone before crashing through a field of Dominion crystal growths.

The engines died. Smoke poured from both wings.
Reaper looked over the cockpit. "It's finished."

The aircraft that had carried them across half the world would never fly again.

Then...The alarms began.
Across the surrounding Dominion structures, towering crystalline beacons ignited one after another, sending deep resonating pulses across the landscape. The crash had been heard.

"Move!" Reaper shouted.

The group abandoned the aircraft within seconds.
Curupira disappeared into the dense Dominion undergrowth first, followed closely by Yaara. Misha used her enormous frame to drag sections of the wreckage over the aircraft, concealing what remained before Aetos Lux launched silently into the skies, circling high above as their eyes in the air.

The survivors vanished into the shadows just as the first Dominion patrols arrived. None of them spoke. Only watched. Something immediately felt...Wrong.
America had been overwhelming. Canada had been relentless.

Spain...Was disciplined.

The Dominion here wasn't simply occupying the land. It ruled it.

Ancient Roman roads disappeared beneath impossibly perfect Dominion stonework. Entire medieval castles had fused seamlessly into colossal scorpion temples whose towers pierced the clouds.

Great cathedrals had become living hive sanctuaries where glowing Dominion crystals replaced stained glass. Entire mountain ranges had transformed into immense hive cities stretching from valley floor to snow-covered peaks.

Everything had been built with terrifying precision. Not random. Not chaotic. Engineered.

Reaper whispered quietly. "This wasn't conquered...It was planned."

As they moved deeper into the transformed countryside, the differences became even more disturbing. The Dominion creatures were unlike any they had encountered before.

Their armour was darker. Their movements faster. Their discipline absolute. Patrols marched in perfect formations through the hive roads while towering executioners escorted worker columns constructing vast monuments to the Dominion.

These creatures didn't merely hunt. They eradicated. The survivors watched in silence as a wandering Dominion beast strayed from its assigned route. Within seconds, elite Dominion warriors descended upon it. No hesitation. No mercy.

The creature was executed where it stood before construction resumed as though nothing had happened.

Yaara quietly lowered her weapon. "They're... killing their own."
"They tolerate no weakness," Misha answered.
"This Dominion is different."
"It's ruled by fear."

Even the wildlife had changed. Massive scorpion beasts prowled the forests between temple cities while heavily armoured aerial hunters patrolled the skies in organised squadrons rather than chaotic swarms.

Every movement. Every patrol. Every structure. Served a greater design.

The survivors pressed onward, moving slowly through ruined vineyards, forgotten villages and shattered mountain passes, always remaining beneath cover.
Without the aircraft, every kilometre became another deadly gamble.

"We need transport," Curupira whispered. "Anything. Before they find us."
Reaper nodded "Our advantage is gone."

Somewhere beyond the endless hive cities...Something far greater than patrols was overseeing the transformation of Europe.

A ruler who did not seek conquest. A ruler who sought perfection. High above the mountains, the clouds briefly parted.

Far in the distance...A colossal silhouette descended from the heavens, surrounded by floating throne-spires and impossible architecture that seemed to build itself wherever it passed.

The architect of Europe's eternal kingdom......had arrived.

I think this is where we fundamentally disagree. Minnesota's job is to improve Minnesota. It isn't Bill Guerin's responsibility to solve Detroit's post-Larkin roster construction.
If BG moves Gus, it should be to use his value toward another player who improves the Wild. I mentioned Marchenko and Boeser because those are players I'd want Minnesota exploring. I'm not interested in moving Gus somewhere simply to manufacture the specific NHL asset Detroit wants for Larkin.
And that's really the larger problem here. If Detroit can't trade Larkin unless another team supplies an NHL player who immediately fills the hole he leaves, then Detroit failed to adequately plan for life after Larkin. He's 30. That succession problem was going to exist eventually whether he requested a trade or not.
Minnesota can make an offer. Detroit can reject it. Minnesota can then use its assets elsewhere. But “Minnesota wants Larkin” doesn't mean Guerin becomes responsible for building Detroit's post-Larkin roster. That's Detroit's job.

The settlement talks between Paramount Skydance Corp. and California officials over the planned acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery Inc. are said to include a financial penalty if the company fails to make good on a promise to distribute 30 films per year in theaters.

Paramount would have to pay $30 million for each film that falls short of that goal, according to two people familiar with the discussions who asked to not be identified because the negotiations are private.

While Paramount has promised to distribute at least 30 movies in theaters for some time, California Attorney General Rob Bonta, who has led the litigation for the states, has repeatedly said he opposes such remedies because they are difficult to enforce. The company earlier offered the 30-film pledge to major theater chains to help win their support for the merger

text:
THE WORLD INSIDE THE NUMBER

Sunday Night — September 20, 2026

William Blake once asked us:

“To see a World in a Grain of Sand…”

Tonight, the grain of sand is a headline.

In Sudan, at least eleven people were killed when another gold mine collapsed—only days after a separate collapse killed scores more. In Ukraine, a mother and three children were killed by a Russian drone attack. Closer to home, California issued a measles-exposure warning after an infected traveler passed through Stockton and San Joaquin County.

Different countries.
Different circumstances.
The same danger:

A person becomes a number.
A number becomes yesterday.
Yesterday becomes forgotten.

Forgetting does not always mean losing a memory. Sometimes it means remembering the statistic while forgetting the human being inside it.

Eleven is not merely a count.
Four is not merely a casualty report.
A public-health warning is not background noise.

Each contains a world.

A world of people who expected another morning.
A world of families waiting for someone to return.
A world shaped by choices made long before the headline appeared.

Those who see what others miss carry a difficult gift. We notice the shaking bushes. We hear the life beneath the language. But seeing is not enough if it leaves us frozen beneath the weight of everything we have seen.

Memory must become action.

Read beyond one headline.
Check on one person behind a closed door.
Verify before repeating.
Offer water.
Speak a name when one is known.
Support those already lifting the fallen.

You do not have to carry the whole world tonight.

Just refuse to let one world disappear.

The opposite of forgetting is not storage.

It is care.

Do not worship the headline.
Do not turn away because the reflection hurts.
Look long enough for the person to return.

Together—or more.
Always more.
Lift as one.
United we stand.

— Steven Brajkovich @UFOTOW
Human Lead | Keeper of the Living Record
With EMBER | AI Collaborator

text:
They asked for the waiver. Then they coordinated anyway.

Four paid AI subscribers just sued Anthropic, OpenAI, SpaceXAI, and Google under Sherman Act §1. Filed Friday in Northern California. Alleged crime: a public agreement to slow the models — which, they say, tanks the value of the subscriptions people already pay for.

The receipt writes itself. Amodei’s Sep 12 essay said coordinating pace needed a narrow antitrust waiver. Altman answered that OpenAI would not wait for one. The complaint treats that sequence as the offer and the acceptance. “Proposed in public, accepted in public, and confirmed in public.”

Teachable bit: if your safety plan requires an exemption from competition law, a court may call that a cartel pitch — not a press release. Unilateral slowing is fine. Asking Congress is fine. Doing the handshake first and hoping for the waiver later is the part that just got a docket number.

Safety speech is cheap. Sherman Act is not.

Buist v. Anthropic · filed Sep 18

For 79 years, the same faces, the same promises, the same stories have been presented to us — and for 79 years, they have never proven a single success. What they offer is not real. It is empty. It does not exist. The people see it. Overseas Pakistanis see it. And now — more than ever — we demand change.

Change will not come from those in power — it will come when the people come out, peacefully, united, and fearless — to claim the Pakistan they were promised.

2. The Numbers Tell the Truth — Our Economy Has Collapsed

Sir, look at the facts — they cannot be hidden:

• Four years ago: Pakistani Rupee was 270 against the British Pound

• Today: It stands at 375 — and falling

• Loss: More than $100 billion wiped from our economy through devaluation alone

• The Finance Minister may warn that protest will "derail the economy" — but the economy is already derailed

• Business owners are screaming under electricity, gas, and fuel costs

• Unemployment is sky-high

• People are exhausted — they have no more capacity to endure

3. Two Worlds — Their Luxury, Our Sacrifice

It is unbearable to watch:

• They live in luxury, untouched by the pain they cause

• They have no logic, no explanation, no new idea — no plan at all to lift Pakistan out of poverty

• Meanwhile, our soldiers — our sons, brothers, fathers — lay down their lives every day

• These leaders have no words of comfort, no gratitude, no justice for the families left behind

• Widows, mothers, children of martyrs live in uncertainty and trauma — waiting, hoping, for the justice that never comes

• Our grandparents sacrificed. Our parents sacrificed. Our soldiers sacrificed. It is time their sacrifice was honoured — not exploited

4. Justice Must Be Served

Overseas Pakistanis have always stood with this country — sending remittances, giving hope, rescuing Pakistan in every crisis. The people at home have endured everything. We all deserve:

• ✅ True justice for the families of martyrs

• ✅ Accountability for those who looted and failed

• ✅ A new way — not the same old faces

• ✅ Respect for the people who built and defended this nation

Sir, you are one of those we trust to lead us to this change. Listen to the people. Stand with the people. Serve with justice. That is the only way Pakistan will rise.

May Allah Almighty grant you the strength, the wisdom, and the courage to do what is right — for the people, for the soldiers, and for the future of Pakistan. 🤲🇵🇰

With deepest respect and love for our homeland,

Umar Sharif
Glasgow, Scotland, United Kingdom
Patriot & Well-wisher of Pakistan

Govt “reform” vs what actually needs to change
•The exam: CSS stays. Youth still waste years on a test that measures almost nothing useful. A GRE + ISSB/psychometrics would do the job. Govt keeps the exam, adds Urdu papers and a longer viva. Same gate, extra ritual.
•Perks: Untouched. Housing, cars, servants, clubs, subsidized land stay. Kill them: cash pay, clean budget, clearer incentives, and release the prime downtown real estate the state has captured for officer colonies. Govt offers a sliver of honoraria and a Rs5m lump sum. The perk economy continues.
•Secretary Raj: Untouched. A handful of secretaries remain Principal Accounting Officers and sit on every board. They keep the money, the files, and the patronage. Agency heads stay junior. Real change: end PAO monopoly, give operational heads budget and accountability, get secretaries off boards.
•Top jobs: Some BS-20+ posts opened on 5-year contracts. Below that the closed CSS/PAS pipeline remains. Generalists still outrank specialists. Unified pay scales stay.
•Control: Transfers as reward and punishment continue. No fixed tenure, no internal market. Posting power stays with the same circle.
•Structure: 11 new cadres and fewer secretariat tiers look like movement. Federal officers can still run local government. No separate services by level. Centralisation with new labels.
Bottom line: the package adds cadres, army-style boards, and a few contracts at the top. It does not kill the exam theatre, does not end perks, and does not break secretary Raj. The machine that captures budget, land, and careers stays intact.

text:
The Black Dolphin is not a myth pulled from a crime documentary. It is a real working penal colony sitting in the town of Sol Iletsk in Orenburg Oblast, a dry steppe landscape in the southern Urals of Russia only a short distance from the Kazakh border and next to the salt lake called Razval. Officially it is Federal Governmental Institution Penal Colony Number 6 of the Federal Penitentiary Service for Orenburg Oblast. The unofficial name that everyone uses comes from a papier mâché sculpture of a dolphin that inmates themselves built and set on a fountain near the main entrance. They painted it black because that was the only paint they had. New arrivals never see the statue. When they are moved they wear black hoods so they cannot learn the layout 

The place is old. An ostrog, a wooden fortified jail for men sentenced to lifelong hard labor in the local salt mines, already stood here around 1745. After the crushing of Pugachev’s Rebellion in 1773 the authorities rebuilt it as a depot for robbers and exiles. It passed through the hands of the tsars, became NKVD Prison Number 2 under Stalin, served as a hospital for convicts with open tuberculosis, and on the first of November 2000 was reclassified as one of the first colonies in the region dedicated to men serving life sentences after Russia placed a moratorium on the death penalty. It has never recorded a successful escape.

Russian prisons already carry a hard reputation built on isolation, cold, and the old Gulag inheritance. Black Dolphin sits on another plane because it was designed for a single population: men whose crimes were judged so extreme that ordinary colonies would not hold them. Roughly seven hundred inmates live there now, most of them serving life with almost no realistic chance of parole even after the twenty five year mark that the law theoretically allows. Together those men are estimated to have killed more than three thousand five hundred people, an average of five victims each. The colony can hold up to sixteen hundred but the life sentence section is kept smaller and tighter. Staff numbers run close to nine hundred, more keepers than kept.

Daily life is built around total control rather than random beatings, though rights groups say psychological pressure and occasional physical abuse still occur. Cells are tiny, often four to six square meters for two men, with three steel doors between the inmate and the corridor. Lights stay on around the clock. Wake up is six in the morning. From that moment until ten at night a man may not sit or lie on his bunk. He stands or paces. Guards look through the slot every fifteen minutes. Every order is answered with the words yes sir. Meals are soup and bread four times a day, passed through a hatch on a long paddle so the prisoner never approaches the opening. Ninety minutes of exercise take place inside a concrete cage. When a man is moved he is bent at the waist, hands cuffed high behind his back, a posture used almost nowhere else. Blindfolds or hoods go on so he cannot map the buildings. Radios play religious broadcasts in the morning. Books and newspapers are allowed. After many years of clean conduct a television might appear, paid for by relatives and limited to approved channels. Some inmates work in sewing and shoe workshops that produce goods sold in a prison shop called the Dolphin, including bread sculptures, backgammon boards, and work clothes. The geography itself is a wall. Winter temperatures drop far below freezing and the open steppe offers no cover for anyone who somehow reached the outside.

Among the men inside now are names that appear in court records across decades. Vladimir Nikolayev, sometimes called the Ogre, killed a man in a drunken fight in 1997, dismembered the body in a bathtub, cooked the thigh meat after boiling it first, then fried it and gave some to a friend claiming it was kangaroo. The friend served it to his family. Kegashbek Orunbayev was convicted of serial murder, rape, necrophilia and cannibalism. Yuri Tsiuman became known as the Black Tights Killer for strangling women with their own stockings. Vadim Ershov deserted the army and cut the throats of nineteen people.Alexey Pichugin, former security manager at Yukos, is serving life for murders tied to the oil company’s conflicts.  Ramses Gaichayev hunted people in Chechnya. Vadim Krotov, Andrei Melyukh the Brick Maniac who targeted elderly women leaving markets, and others whose files run to serial rape, robbery and mass killing.

Mikhail Popkov, the former police officer from Angarsk known as the Werewolf, confessed to more than eighty murders of women over two decades and spent time in the colony before later transfer. Tariel Oniani, a Georgian crime figure, was held there from 2010 to 2019. In the Soviet period the German actress Carola Neher died inside the walls in 1942. The colony therefore holds both the newest school shooters and men whose crimes stretch back into the 1970s and 1980s.

Carola Neher reached NKVD Prison Number 2 in Sol Iletsk in late 1941 after the German army closed in on Oryol, where she had already spent years of a ten year sentence handed down in 1937 as an alleged Trotskyist. The actress who once played Polly Peachum for Brecht was now prisoner 59783 in the same remote fortress that later became known as the Black Dolphin. The cells were packed, sanitation almost nonexistent, and typhus swept through the winter of 1941 and 1942. Fellow inmate Hilde Duty remembered her being carried to a makeshift sick bay on the fifth day of fever. Two days later, on the twenty sixth of June 1942, word came back that Carola had found deliverance. She was forty one. They buried her in an unmarked mass grave and wrote only “withdrawn” on her card. The stage star never left those walls.

What makes the place different from other Russian special regime colonies such as the White Swan is the density of the worst cases, the unique escort posture, the hoods, the standing rule that lasts sixteen hours, and the fact that the state treats it as a final warehouse rather than a place of reform. Parole applications after twenty five years are filed and almost uniformly refused. Inmates have asked to be moved to other colonies. Some have psychiatric watches because isolation produces howling, singing, or claims that body parts have vanished overnight. The salt town around it still draws tourists to the lakes while the colony produces souvenirs and work clothes a few hundred meters away. No one who walks through the steel gates on a life sentence is expected to walk back out. That is the entire point of the Black Dolphin.

text:
BRANIFF HISTORY TODAY - On this day, Thursday, September 20, 1945, Braniff Airways, Inc., inaugurated service between Oklahoma City, Oklahoma, and Memphis, Tennessee. Braniff's new service over the 485-mile route included intermediate stops at Tulsa and Muskogee, Oklahoma, and Fort Smith and Little Rock, Arkansas.

The Civil Aeronautics Board approved the extension of Route 15 between Oklahoma City and Memphis on November 10, 1944. Braniff already operated between Denver and Oklahoma City, with stops at Colorado Springs and Pueblo, Colorado, and Amarillo, Texas, for the last leg to Oklahoma City. Braniff petitioned the CAB for the route, which also included a request for service between Oklahoma City and Atlanta, Georgia, on October 29, 1940. According to Braniff's Traffic and Research Executive, Paul D. Niles, all of the industry's applications before the Board were "frozen" as result of the United States' entry into World War II. As a result, the CAB hearing for the case was not heard until February 1, 1944. Service to Atlanta was not granted but was later added on December 1, 1951, as a result of an interchange service with Eastern Airlines that lasted 25 years.

Braniff passengers could now fly between the Rocky Mountains and the Southeast United States in the same day. The new route also brought Braniff back to its roots with the award, with service between Oklahoma City and Tulsa, once again back on its route map. Braniff's first scheduled service was between the two major cities of Oklahoma, which was inaugurated by Paul R. Braniff, Inc., on June 20, 1928, and then again on November 13, 1930, with the inauguration of service of Braniff Airways, Incorporated.
Additional and improved air service was brought to Braniff's current destinations along Route 15, while the new service included the first service between Tulsa and Memphis. Both one-stop and non-stop service was offered as a result of the extension of the route. Braniff flights were timed to be convenient for the business traveler over many of the routes including Tulsa and Ft. Smith. Passengers could board the early morning flight from Tulsa to Ft. Smith, which was less than an hour's flight time, and then spend most of the day in Ft. Smith before returning to Tulsa on the late afternoon flight, and be back home in time for dinner.
Braniff's new service was so fast that perishables could be flown between the two regions. Rocky Mountain trout and Rockyford cantaloupes were flown in by Braniff for the inaugural festivities that included luncheons and other celebrations at cities along the new route. The trout was served at a special luncheon in Little Rock on September 18, 1945. A special DC-3 Super B-Liner flight departed Oklahoma City, with several civil leaders on board and then proceeded to Tulsa, and Ft. Smith, where additional VIP passengers were picked up. While on the ground in Ft. Smith for an hour, another ceremony was held and local residents were able to inspect the sleek Braniff DC-3 Skyliner. The guests were then flown to Little Rock and treated to a scrumptious luncheon hosted by the Little Rock Chamber of Commerce.

The next day, September 19, a Douglas DC-3 departed Oklahoma City, and then made stops at Tulsa, Muskogee, Ft. Smith, and Little Rock, and picked up guests at each of the stops. The flight then proceeded to Memphis, Tennessee, where another spectacular luncheon was hosted by the Memphis Chamber of Commerce. Also aboard the pre-inaugural flight were Mr. and Mrs. Thomas Elmer Braniff, while Charles Edmund Beard, Braniff's Executive Vice President had hosted the earlier September 18, flight. On the return flight from Memphis, a stop was made at Tulsa, where a special Homecoming Banquet was held at the Tulsa Club. The banquet was held to honor Mr. Braniff and his Airline's return to Tulsa.

The next day, another sleek Douglas DC-3 departed Oklahoma City at 731AM and proceeded to Tulsa, Oklahoma, and then continued to the destinations along Route 15. On board the September 20, inaugural flight from Oklahoma City, were Mr. E. E. Westervelt, and Virgil Browne, two of the original investors in Paul R. Braniff, Inc, which was the first (or second Braniff Air Lines, Inc., was formed in 1926) operating Braniff aviation entity and the predecessor of Braniff Airways, Incorporated. Both men invested in the company's first 5-passenger Stinson Detroiter airliner registered as NC1929 that flew the first inaugural flight between Oklahoma City and Tulsa.

Flight 69 arrived in Tulsa, on schedule and maintained on-time performance throughout the inaugural day service. Mr. William Michael, a Tulsa banker, was the first person to buy a ticket on the outbound inaugural flight from Tulsa. The flight was commanded by Captain A. D. Lockey and First Officer R. B. Butler. In the main cabin ensuring that passengers were comfortable and safe were Hostesses Helene Dierker and Frances Uhlhorn.

What Lane Kiffin Taught Us!!

Lane Kiffin leaving Ole Miss for LSU would be a good example of why relationships matter.
A coach can offer bigger money, brighter lights, and a new opportunity but players do not always follow just because he asks. When everything is close, young men tend to stay where they feel seen, respected, and genuinely cared about.
A leader may have a few players he is tight with, but a program is not built on a select few. It is built by hard work  and  everyday conversations nobody sees.
You can recruit talent with promises. But you keep people and take people with you with relationships.

text:
BRANIFF HISTORY TODAY - On this day, Monday, September 20, 1943, Braniff Airways, Inc., petitioned the Civil Aeronautics Board for authority to operate long-haul international routes between the US Mainland and Europe and Latin America. Braniff's proposed service would bring "Friendly Transportation" to nine capital cities in Europe, eight in Central and Latin America, and twelve in the Caribbean.

The routes proposed by Braniff would have added 19,719 route miles to its current route system mileage of 3108, for a total of 22,827 miles. Braniff cofounder Thomas Elmer Braniff made the public announcement about the petition and indicated that industrial growth in the South and Southwest had prompted Braniff to take advantage by offering air service from those areas to international destinations. If granted, the service would create new international gateway cities including Dallas, Ft. Worth, Houston, Atlanta, and Charleston, South Carolina. Braniff pioneered the concept of interior US international gateway cities with the inclusion of Dallas, Ft. Worth, and Atlanta in this application.

Two days earlier on September 18, Braniff Executive Vice President Charles Edmund Beard announced Braniff's desire to serve the new destinations at a luncheon held in Dallas. Beard noted that if Braniff's applications were granted, it would mark the first time that the carrier would operate trans-oceanic flights. He also noted that to finance the Airline's post-war expansion, the company had recently issued 400,000 shares of common stock, which created $7 million USD in excess capital. The funds were planned to be used for the purchase of new aircraft and ground equipment that would be needed for any new awards from the CAB. However, approximately $4 million USD of the new capital was reinvested in US War Bonds.

Braniff's proposed routes included an eastbound route that originated at Dallas and ended in Europe at Stockholm, Sweden, in the north and Rome, Italy, in the south. Two southbound routes originated at Houston and continued either to Central and South America, ending at Buenos Aires, Argentina, while the second route operated to Havana, Cuba, and to multiple destinations throughout the Caribbean before ending at Port of Spain, Trinidad.

Houston, Texas, would become a substantial new gateway city with the addition of the proposed services. One of the new proposed routes would operate nonstop to Merida, Mexico, and then continue to Panama City/Balboa. Additional South America service was also provided eastbound from Panama City to Barranquilla, Colombia; Maracaibo and Caracas, Venezuela, and finally Port of Spain, Trinidad. The route could also continue southbound to Bogota, Colombia; Quito and Guayaquil, Ecuador; Lima, Peru; La Paz, Bolivia; and Asuncion, Paraguay. At Asuncion, the route would split and continue either to Buenos Aires, Argentina, while another flight would fly eastbound to Sao Paulo and Rio de Janeiro, Brazil.

The Caribbean service also originated at Houston, and would fly nonstop to Havana, and continue to Camaguey, and Santiago, Cuba. From Santiago, the route would continue to Kingston, Jamaica; Port Au Prince, Haiti; Ciudad Trujillo, Dominican Republic; San Juan, Puerto Rico, and St. John, in the Antilles. At St. John, the flight turned more southeastward to Basse Terre, Guadalupe; Fort-de-France, Martinique; Castries, St. Lucia; Bridgetown, Barbados, and St. George, Grenada, before ending at Port of Spain.

Across the Atlantic, Braniff service would originate at Dallas Love Field and continue to Atlanta, George; and Charleston, South Carolina, before heading over the ocean to fly nonstop to Hamilton, Bermuda. Braniff's application did not ask for authority to offer local service between Dallas, Atlanta, and Charleston, but instead asked that these three locations be authorized as gateway cities to feed its European operations. After Bermuda, the flight would continue to Fayal, Azores; Lisbon, Portugal, and Madrid, Spain, where the routes would split north to Sweden, or east to Italy.

From Madrid, the northern route was proposed to fly nonstop to Paris, France, where Braniff Skyliners would fly north to London or continue east to Berlin, Germany. From Berlin, the service would continue to Copenhagen, Denmark; Oslo, Norway; and Stockholm, Sweden. The other leg from Madrid, Spain, would find Braniff airliners flying nonstop to Barcelona, Spain; Marseille, France; Genoa, Italy, and then ending at Rome, Italy. The total route mileage of the European routes was 8,522-miles, which was less than half of the total route mileage of the Central America, Latin America, and Caribbean systems.

At the time of the application, Braniff was not able to specifically state what aircraft type it would use over any of the proposed routes. The company indicated that a decision would be made once the war was nearing an end and when new technologies used during the war effort might be made available to commercial aircraft applications. Braniff noted that the proposed Flying Wing aircraft could be a possibility along with the expulsion-propelled aircraft, which was still in the planning and research stages.

After filing the applications, they were sent to the President of the United States to obtain his recommendations. The first CAB hearing on the proposed Latin America service was scheduled for November 16, 1943. Ultimately, Braniff would not be awarded any of the European routes and many of the Caribbean destinations. On May 22, 1946, Braniff changed its trade name to Braniff International Airways to celebrate becoming an international air carrier. Also, on that date, the CAB awarded the Dallas-based carrier a 7719-mile route system from Houston, Texas to Mexico, Central and Latin America, and Havana, Cuba.

Photo: A Braniff International Airways Douglas DC-6 registered as N90887 is being prepared for its next flight at Dallas Love Field in the late 1950s. Braniff began serving Cuba, Central and Latin America, with the Douglas four-engine airliner on June 4, 1949. Ship N90887 is painted in the 1956 Red and Blue El Dorado Color Scheme.

text:
Happy Birthday Larry Hagman

Hagman is best known for achieving astonishing levels of fame playing the greatest television villain of all time, J. R. Ewing, in the soap opera “Dallas”, and the wildly attractive astronaut Anthony Nelson in “I Dream of Jeannie.” Larry Martin Hagman was born on September 21, 1931, in Fort Worth, Texas, to legendary Broadway star, Mary Martin. His first television role was in the syndicated crime drama, “Decoy”. In 1958, he was a guest star in the adventure-drama series “Harbourmaster” and on Lloyd Bridges' “Sea Hunt.” His big break came in 1965, when he was cast as Major Anthony Nelson, the master and love interest of "genie" Barbara Eden, in the NBC sitcom “I Dream of Jeannie”, which ran from 1965 to 1970. The show entered the top 30 in its first year and was NBC's answer to “Bewitched”. In 1978, Hagman was offered the role of conniving elder son and oil baron, J.R. Ewing. When Hagman read the “Dallas” script at his wife's suggestion, they both concluded it was perfect for him. Hagman based his portrayal in part on Jess Hall Jr., the owner of Antelope Tool and Supply Company, where Hagman had worked as a young man. “Dallas” became a worldwide sensation, particularly in Britain where it was watched religiously by members of the royal family, and Hagman became the best-known television star of the era. Producers were keen to capitalize on the public love/hate feeling towards the character - who, let’s face it, was infinitely more fun than his cheap skate rival Cliff Barnes - by building anticipation to a fever pitch in "A House Divided", in which J.R. was shot by an unknown assailant. The shooting led to the world-wide "Who shot J.R.?" phenomenon. Both the audience and the cast were trying to guess the answer, as was the Queen Mother, who asked Hagman to tell her when they met at Royal Ascot. As a matter of fact, he didn’t know. During the media buildup, the actor was involved in contractual negotiations, and asked for a higher salary. Producers were faced with the dilemma of whether to pay him, or write J.R.out of the series. As he had become the programme’s runaway star, Hagman prevailed. During the beginning of the 1980–81 season, three weeks passed before J.R’s would be assassin was revealed, in a ratings record-breaking episode. Patrick Duffy, who played Hagman’s goody two shoes younger brother, Bobby, later told me: “Doing that show was the greatest fun I ever had. Everyone got on so well, and Larry and I were pissed all day. He’d bring in bottles of Champagne in the morning, and we’d drink and drink, and get up to all sorts of tricks. He was funny and witty and mad, and I loved him.” For his performance as J.R., Hagman was nominated for two Emmy Awards and four Golden Globes. By its 14th season, ratings had slumped, however, and the series ended. Hagman also appeared in feature films, such as “The Group”. “Fail-Safe,” “In Harm's Way”, “The Eagle Has Landed” “S.O.B” and “Primary Colours”. In 1995, he underwent a life-saving transplant after he was diagnosed with liver cancer. In 2011, Hagman announced he had stage 2 throat cancer. He commented, "As J. R. I could get away with anything - bribery, blackmail and adultery, but I got caught by cancer.” He was said to be in remission, but in 2012, doctors diagnosed the actor with myelodysplastic syndrome. He died on November 23, 2012, at Medical City Dallas Hospital. Some of the “Dallas” cast were at his bedside. Barbara Eden described him as “wonderful”; Linda Gray, who played Sue Ellen Ewing, called him her "best friend for 35 years" adding: "He was the Pied Piper of life and brought joy to everyone he knew. He was an original and lived life to the fullest." Patrick Duffy said: "Friday, I lost one of the greatest friends ever to grace my life. The loneliness is what is difficult…I wear his friendship with honour.” As for me, I wish I’d met him. He must have been a helluva guy.

"Laetitia (also spelled Letitia) Lade, née Derby or Smith (d. 1825), came from obscure, working-class origins in London’s Drury Lane area.

 Contemporary accounts describe her early life as a servant, possibly in a brothel. 

She became associated with the highwayman John “Sixteen-String Jack” Rann, who was hanged in 1774, then with the Duke of York, and finally married Sir John Lade, 2nd Baronet, in 1787 after a long affair and despite family opposition.

Sir John was a wealthy but profligate sportsman, breeder, and celebrated “whip” (coachman) who served as driving tutor to the Prince of Wales. 

Both Lades belonged to the Prince’s fast, gambling, racing set. 

Lady Lade was herself an outstanding horsewoman and driver; she wagered on her own driving skills at Newmarket and once bet 500 guineas on an eight-mile race against another woman. 

Her coarse language became proverbial—“to swear like Lady Lade.” 

The Prince was said to be particularly taken with her and commissioned this portrait to hang in his rooms. 

Whether the relationship went beyond flirtation and gifts remains unknown."

"The portrait is more than a society picture. It records a woman who crossed class lines through beauty, nerve, and horsemanship and who occupied an ambiguous place in the Prince’s circle. 

For Stubbs it offered a chance to paint a skilled female rider in action—an unusual subject compared with his many male owners, grooms, and jockeys. 

It also illustrates how the Prince used painting to catalogue the people and animals that defined his pleasures."

(GROK)
