I think I have to switch from omp to deepseek because dsh runs everything in the harness through a central event bus. 

Two months ago (I have document time stamps, I swear!) I was already sketching a vision of an agent/harness that had "interceptors", extremely fast inference that I can put between anything. Sending tool call? Interceptor. Result of tool call? Interceptor? After I hit enter key but before my message is sent to the api? Interceptor. 

I already prototyped the parts for passive memory retrieval, before every agent turn I send recent history to an embeddings model and get similarity hits for the entire corpus of my conversation history. I'd retrieve the hits + surrounding messages, judge them against the input, rerank them(probably not one single ranking).

Then I would inject a little system message with low pressure "offers", like "similar conversations have happened before here and here", maybe with a tiny summary and a canonical source link so the original could be retrieved. Once that machinery works I can hook up other stuff like curated knowkedgesets. 

I would want interceptors on tool calls and edits and stuff. If the edit failed for a stupid reason why can't I just have it be rewritten instead of demanding more attention from my main agent? 

I've been building a context window manager that doesn't compact, it renders a materialized view, treating the transcript as an immutable event log. I already used a tiny local model to classify turns and extract topics. Adjacent turns with topics in common get linked into an epoch. Then you know you can drop epochs all once after the topic moves on. 

Objects dropped out of view get replaced with a tombstone that has a topic list/summary/recall instructions. 

Epochs also get recorded in the transcript, so the history becomes a skip list, which makes later retrieval easier. 

I was content to just slowly chip away at this stuff but all of these ideas are exactly jev-shaped so now I have to lock in. 

(first attempt at topic extraction, comparing every turn against its neighbors:)

text:
Since sacks became an official NFL stat in 1982, no linebacker had ever done this in one game.

8+ tackles. 2 interceptions. A sack. A touchdown.

Today Devin Lloyd did it. For Carolina. 17 months after the team that drafted him declined his fifth year option.

Here is the full line from the Panthers 34-3 win in Atlanta:

9 tackles. 2 tackles for loss. 1 sack. 3 passes defensed. 2 interceptions. 1 touchdown.

Eight of those tackles came in the FIRST HALF.

Then he got going.

In the third quarter he picked off Cooper Rush and ran it back 53 yards. One man away from the end zone.

Atlanta pulled Rush. In came Jack Strand, an undrafted rookie out of Division II Minnesota State Moorhead, making his NFL debut.

Strand's first NFL pass got tipped by Jaycee Horn.

Lloyd caught it and took it to the house.

"I knew I was going to score on the second one."

Rough welcome for a kid who threw 126 touchdowns in college. He will have better days.

Dave Canales has been coaching in the NFL for 17 years.

"I don't know if I've seen a better performance out of a linebacker in 17 years of coaching in the NFL."

Bryce Young, who threw three touchdowns himself, used one word for it. "Surreal."

Now rewind.

Devin Lloyd grew up in Chula Vista, California. Both of his parents served in the United States Navy.

At Otay Ranch High School he played receiver, safety AND punter. He once had four interceptions in a single game.

He was a three star recruit. Utah was his only Power Five offer.

He redshirted. He was a backup. Then he became a starter.

His senior year he led the Pac-12 in sacks and returned an interception for a touchdown in the Pac-12 Championship Game. Consensus All-American. 27th pick in the 2022 draft, Jacksonville.

He was solid there. Defensive Rookie of the Month his first September. Over 100 tackles in each of the next two seasons.

Then in April 2025, the Jaguars declined his fifth year option.

If you do not follow contracts, that is a team saying we are not ready to lock you in yet. Go play your final year and we will see.

He knew exactly what that meant.

"At this point now I know this is effectively a one-year prove-it deal."

So he proved it.

Two interceptions of Brock Purdy in Week 4. AFC Defensive Player of the Week.

Week 5, Monday Night Football, he picked off Patrick Mahomes at the goal line and ran it back 99 YARDS. Longest pick six in Jaguars history. Jacksonville won by three.

Five interceptions on the season. Pro Bowl. Second team All-Pro.

Then he hit free agency, and Carolina gave him three years, $45 million, $25 million guaranteed.

To be fair to Jacksonville, they did try to keep him.

"There was an offer on the table," Lloyd said.

He took Carolina's.

His new teammate Jaelan Phillips has been saying the same thing since OTAs.

"He's the best football player I've played with."

After today, Phillips went further.

"To me he's a gold jacket guy, man. I'm honored to be on the same field as him."

That is a heavy thing to say in Carolina. The greatest linebacker in Panthers history, Luke Kuechly, just got his gold jacket.

Nobody is saying Lloyd is Kuechly. It is Week 2. Atlanta was playing without its top two quarterbacks and finished the day with an undrafted rookie.

But in 44 years of counting sacks, no linebacker had put up that line against anybody.

A three star kid from a Navy family with one Power Five offer just did it in his second game with his new team.

Somewhere in Jacksonville, somebody is looking at that fifth year option again.

text:
Reggie Bush says Vince Young was offered his 2005 Heisman Trophy by the NCAA after USC was stripped of its wins and Vince declined it because he believed it would always be Reggie’s trophy

“What’s crazy, you know what I love about the game? Sometimes the players who are your rivals or your enemies on the field end up becoming some guys you’re close homies with. Vince is somebody I have a lot of respect for because Vince also did something that I’ll never forget.”

“After we played the national championship game, obviously they beat us. One of the things that we did, me and Matt, was we went to their locker room. We sought out Vince and the coach, wanted to shake their hands, like, ‘Yo, congrats. That was a good-ass game.’”

“After that, when these penalties were happening and the Heisman Trust stripped me of the Heisman Trophy, one of the things that they did was they went to Vince and they asked him if he wanted the trophy.”

“They took the trophy from me, and they were going to give it to Vince. Vince says to the Heisman Trust, ‘That’s Reggie’s trophy.’”

“I’ll never forget that because you gotta think, first of all, he just beat us. They’re on top of the world. They just took down the number one team. He would have every right in that moment, if he wanted to, to be like, ‘Absolutely. Let me get that.’”

“That respect and that bond that you create on that battlefield, on the football field, you can’t break that. Shout out to Vince. That’s my dog. I have a lot of respect for him, not only as a football player, but just as a man and everything he stands for.”

“For the decision that he made as a young kid, young 20-, 21-year-old kid, to make that decision and to say that and to support me in that time, that meant everything to me.”

Coming to Understand Tether in Bessent's Economic Fury Tactics

🧭 How does Treasury isolate Iran when Iran moves hundreds of millions of dollars in bitcoin? The answer is within USDT.

💵 What is USDT?

USDT is the dollar stablecoin issued by Tether, a private company now headquartered in El Salvador, and it is by a wide margin the most widely used dollar substitute in the crypto economy. Each unit represents a claim on one dollar held in Tether's reserves, and the bulk of those reserves sits in short-dated United States Treasury bills, which makes Tether one of the larger holders of American government debt anywhere, private or sovereign. USDT is not a blockchain of its own. It is a token that Tether issues on other people's blockchains, chiefly Tron, a fast and inexpensive network launched in 2017 by the entrepreneur Justin Sun, and Ethereum, the second-largest blockchain by value.

🧩 Then what is a token?

Bitcoin and ether are what are called native coins, meaning that the blockchain protocol itself keeps the record of who owns them, and no company stands behind that record. A token works differently. It lives inside a smart contract, which is a small program that someone deploys onto a blockchain and which keeps its own internal table of addresses and balances. The blockchain runs that program exactly as written and records every change to its table, but the rules inside the program were written by whoever deployed it. When you hold ether, Ethereum's consensus enforces your balance. When you hold USDT on Ethereum, Tether's program enforces it, and Ethereum simply guarantees that the program ran as Tether wrote it.

⛽ You hold 1,000 USDT on Tron and no TRX. Can you send it?

You cannot. TRX is Tron's native coin, and every instruction you send to Tether's contract consumes computing resources on the network, a charge that blockchains call gas. That fee must be paid in the chain's native coin, so a holder of USDT on Tron must also keep a small balance of TRX, just as a holder of USDT on Ethereum must keep some ether. The token travels on a road owned by someone else, and the toll is paid in that road's currency.

🧊 Tether blacklists your address. Where does the block happen?

The block happens inside Tether's own contract. Tron's validators, the operators who assemble and confirm the network's blocks of transactions, have no role in it. Tether's program contains a blacklist function and a companion function that can destroy a blacklisted balance, and only Tether's administrative key can invoke them. Once an address is marked, the contract refuses every transfer out of it, and although the balance remains visible on the public ledger indefinitely, it can never move again. Bitcoin has no equivalent, because there is no issuer's contract sitting between a bitcoin holder and the protocol, and so no party exists that could freeze a bitcoin address.

🤝 Who owes you the dollar?

Tether owes it to you, and Tron owes you nothing. Tron is only the network the token moves across. If Tron were to fail, you would lose a convenient way to move your USDT, but Tether's obligation to you would remain. If Tether were to fail, the entry in its contract would persist on a perfectly healthy blockchain and would be worth nothing, because the promise behind it would be gone.

🏪 A Tehran merchant takes in 50,000 USDT. Where does he cash out?

He sells it to a local broker or exchange for Iranian rials, and he never deals with Tether at all. Tether redeems tokens for dollars only for verified institutional customers who have passed its know-your-customer checks, confirming their identity and ownership, and who move sums of roughly a hundred thousand dollars or more through Tether's banking partners. Everyone else trades USDT with one another in the secondary market. The merchant's tokens hold their dollar value only because some large institution upstream can buy USDT below a dollar and redeem it with Tether at full value, which keeps the price pinned. The dollar side of a stablecoin therefore lives inside banks and courts, while the token side moves freely across the world, and Iran enjoys the free side only for as long as the banked side permits it.

🌐 Why would a Dubai exchange enforce American sanctions on an Iranian client?

The Office of Foreign Assets Control, a bureau of the Treasury Department known as OFAC, administers American economic sanctions through a published register called the Specially Designated Nationals list. That list names individuals, companies, and ships, and since 2018 it has also named cryptocurrency wallet addresses. American persons may not deal with anyone on the list. The more powerful tool is the secondary sanction, under which a foreign bank or exchange that does business with a listed party can itself be cut off from the United States financial system. For an exchange in Dubai or Istanbul, losing access to dollars would be ruinous, so refusing an Iranian client is the cheaper choice even though no American court has jurisdiction over it.

⚖️ What did Congress add?

In July 2025 Congress passed, and the President signed, the Guiding and Establishing National Innovation for U.S. Stablecoins Act, known as the GENIUS Act, which is the first federal law governing dollar stablecoins. Most coverage focused on its reserve requirements, but one clause concerning foreign issuers matters most for this question. It provides that a stablecoin from a foreign issuer may be offered to Americans only if that issuer has the technological capability to comply, and will comply, with the terms of any lawful order. Tether is a foreign issuer, so the blacklist function in its contract became the condition of access to the American market rather than a courtesy extended at Tether's discretion. The Act also expressly preserved the Treasury Secretary's existing power to block stablecoin transactions, and it treats stablecoin issuers as financial institutions under the Bank Secrecy Act, the same anti-money-laundering reporting regime that governs banks. The Act's outright prohibition on selling non-compliant stablecoins to Americans takes effect in July 2028. In the meantime Treasury is writing the implementing rules: the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network, Treasury's anti-money-laundering bureau, joined OFAC in proposing a sanctions-compliance rule for issuers in April 2026, and Treasury issued a further proposed rule in August 2026.

₿ Iran moves bitcoin. How did Treasury answer?

On September 17, 2026, Treasury reported that a network run by Babak Zanjani, an Iranian businessman whom Washington first sanctioned in 2013 for helping Tehran sell oil around the international embargo, had transferred hundreds of millions of dollars in bitcoin to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, the military and security organization that also controls a large share of Iran's economy. Treasury did not freeze that bitcoin, because it had no means to do so. It designated the businesses through which the bitcoin had to pass. In June 2026, under a sanctions campaign Treasury named Economic Fury, OFAC designated Nobitex, Iran's largest cryptocurrency exchange, together with three other Iranian exchanges and Nobitex's chairman. In September, under a broader government-wide campaign called Operation Economic Outcast, OFAC designated BitBank, a digital-asset venture controlled by Zanjani. These actions rest on Executive Order 13902, a 2020 order that allows sanctions against whole sectors of the Iranian economy, and which the administration has now applied to Iran's digital-asset sector by name.

🚪 Where does bitcoin fail Iran?

Bitcoin fails Iran at the points where it must be converted into something else, which traders call the on-ramps and off-ramps. Bitcoin is very good at holding and moving value that no government can seize. It is poor at paying a Chinese supplier an invoice fixed in dollars, because its price moves too much between the day a contract is signed and the day it is paid, and it does nothing to steady the rial. Sooner or later every conversion runs through a person or a firm, and people and firms can be placed on the Specially Designated Nationals list.

🎚️ Why would Washington promote stablecoins while sanctioning the people who use them?

Both policies operate the same lever. Every new dollar of USDT in circulation requires Tether to buy more Treasury bills, which helps finance the American government. Every issuer that wants access to American customers must build the freezing mechanism and agree to use it when lawfully ordered. As the informal economies of the world adopt dollar tokens, they become both more dependent on the dollar and more exposed to American enforcement, and the two effects arrive together.

🎯 So does Iran's bitcoin defeat the strategy?

It does not, because the strategy never depended on stopping it. The aim of Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent's campaign, which the White House describes as severing every remaining economic lifeline of the Iranian regime, is to make every usable form of money either freezable or expensive. Once Iran is pushed off stablecoins, it must trade in a volatile bearer asset through unlicensed brokers, and it pays a discount at every conversion. The money continues to flow, but at a steadily rising cost, and every institution willing to handle it becomes a target in its turn. That campaign also sits within National Security Presidential Memorandum 2, the February 2025 directive that instructed Treasury to restore maximum economic pressure on Iran.

🪙 The lesson for anyone who holds sound money is an uncomfortable one. The programmable dollar has proven to be far more controllable than the paper dollar ever was, because every token carries within its own contract the means of stopping it. Inflation and debasement remain real concerns, but the property that now decides whether a form of money is truly yours is whether anyone else can stop your transfer. Bitcoin answers to no issuer. Every token answers to the one that created it.

📚 Sources: GENIUS Act, Public Law 119-27 (https://t.co/9ORkE6ZOI8). U.S. Treasury press releases on Economic Fury (June 2, 2026) and Operation Economic Outcast (September 17, 2026). The White House, Operation Economic Outcast (August 24, 2026). National Security Presidential Memorandum 2 (February 2025).

SUMMARY & CLIFFHANGER

**Houthi missile strikes on Riyadh and Yanbu energy infrastructure have pushed the Middle East toward an unprecedented escalation.**

**This aggressive action targeting sensitive government sites in the Saudi capital and Aramco facilities in Yanbu forced US President Donald Trump to abruptly leave Camp David, signaling that Washington is preparing a massive military response to protect its regional allies and secure the global oil supply.**

GEOPOLITICAL IMPLICATIONS

The security situation in the Persian Gulf has reached a critical threshold following the targeting of the Saudi capital.

The air defense systems of Saudi Arabia, heavily reliant on Western Patriot batteries, faced a severe saturation test as multiple projectiles penetrated deep into sovereign airspace.

This coordinated attack demonstrates a significant advancement in the offensive capabilities, guidance systems, and intelligence gathering of the Yemen-based Houthi group.

The direct threat to major urban centers forces a complete reevaluation of defensive postures across the Arabian Peninsula, indicating that existing defense umbrellas have strategic gaps.

Washington’s rapid response, including the immediate return of the US President to the White House, indicates that military assets in the region are being positioned for immediate retaliatory options.

Any potential kinetic response by Western forces risks drawing other regional actors into a broader confrontation, creating a cycle of escalation that will be extremely difficult to de-escalate.

Energy markets are bracing for severe disruption as the targets included vital Aramco facilities in Yanbu, a key industrial hub.

This strategic port city on the Red Sea coast serves as a crucial alternative route for Saudi oil exports, allowing bypass of the highly vulnerable Strait of Hormuz.

By targeting Yanbu, the offensive directly threatens Saudi Arabia's primary backup export infrastructure, leaving global energy flows deeply exposed to direct interdiction.

The economic impact of this physical vulnerability is immediate, raising risk premiums for maritime transport, insurance, and long-term energy contracts.

• Crude oil futures are expected to spike as traders price in the heightened risk of sustained infrastructure damage and supply disruptions.

• Maritime security operations in the Red Sea will require immediate reinforcement to prevent a prolonged blockade or disruption of critical shipping lanes.

• The vulnerability of desalination plants and processing facilities in the region raises the threat level for local industrial operations.

The attack accelerates the consolidation of new security arrangements and defense pacts across the Middle East.

Turkey has already declared its readiness to meet Saudi military requirements under the newly signed "Mecca Joint Defence Agreement."

This development indicates a shift where regional powers seek to diversify their security partnerships beyond traditional, exclusive Western guarantees.

The failure of diplomatic channels to contain the conflict highlights the growing limitations of international bodies like the United Nations Security Council.

Ankara's offer to provide direct military support to Riyadh redraws the alliance map, positioning Turkey as a major security provider in the Gulf region.

This realignment could dilute US influence in the region, as Middle Eastern capitals actively seek pragmatic, bilateral security arrangements to hedge against a perceived decline in American security guarantees.

SYSTEMIC IMPACT

This confrontation marks a fundamental shift in the global balance of power, revealing the structural limits of US military deterrence in the Middle East.

As regional actors deploy highly precise, low-cost asymmetric weaponry against high-value strategic targets, the traditional security architecture established by Western powers is failing to provide adequate protection.

The emerging security paradigm will likely see increased involvement from regional players like Turkey, alongside a potential expansion of Chinese and Russian diplomatic and military influence as Gulf states seek more reliable security partners.

The long-term stability of the global economy now rests on a highly volatile security environment where energy infrastructure remains permanently vulnerable to asymmetric warfare.

This vulnerability will accelerate the global transition to alternative energy sources while simultaneously forcing major economies to securitize their supply chains against state and non-state threats.

text:
Swatting is already treated as a specific public-safety and cybercrime problem. Since 2023, the FBI has even maintained a national system to correlate incidents across different jurisdictions.

What do police do when they receive the call?

The problem is that at first, they do not know the call is fake. If someone calls saying, “I killed my family, I have hostages, and I’m armed,” the dispatcher cannot simply dismiss it because it seems suspicious. 911 guidelines indicate that it should initially be handled as a real emergency.

However, dispatchers have learned to look for indicators of swatting: the call being the only report of an alleged shooting, a lack of background noise consistent with the claimed situation, unusual or nonexistent Caller ID information, an overly elaborate or scripted-sounding story, changes in the account, abnormally calm behavior from the supposed perpetrator, and so on. None of these factors by itself proves that the call is false.

When an address has previously been identified as a possible target, some dispatch centers may have a note in the CAD system. CISA guidance even recommends having a previously verified phone number for the person and, in certain cases, a verification word or phrase. That way, when a suspicious call comes in, the center can attempt to contact the resident through a known channel before or during the police response.

That does not mean police will simply not respond. Units may still be dispatched because a genuine emergency could occur at an address that had previously been targeted. What changes is that officers may arrive knowing that there is a history of swatting, rather than blindly assuming that an armed murderer is inside the house.

Are these cases actually investigated?

Yes, extensively.

In May 2023, the FBI created the National Common Operating Picture (VCC-NCOP), where law-enforcement agencies can share swatting incidents in near real time. Between May and September 2023, more than 300 incidents had already been recorded. This makes it possible to determine that calls appearing to be isolated incidents across several states may actually originate from the same group.

The FBI issued another specific nationwide alert in April 2025 because of multiple recent incidents, and in August 2026 it reported that during the 2025–2026 school year, authorities had investigated numerous cases involving false threats and swatting attacks against schools.

How do they find the person responsible if the phone number is spoofed?

Caller ID spoofing makes the number displayed to 911 practically useless as a direct means of identification, but it does not necessarily erase the technical trail.

Investigators can reconstruct the chain through VoIP provider records, accounts used, IP addresses, subscription or payment information, associated devices, and email accounts or online platforms involved. The FBI itself explains that even when VoIP calls and spoofed Caller ID are used, providers may still hold information that allows investigators to trace the infrastructure involved.

In addition, many swatters eventually connect those technical traces to their real identities through Discord, Telegram, or other communities, reused aliases, posts in which they brag about attacks, payments, or operational mistakes. In several cases, perpetrators even livestreamed swatting incidents or advertised “swatting-for-hire” services.

VPNs, proxies, VoIP services, and compromised accounts make attribution significantly more difficult, especially when the perpetrator is located in another country, but they do not make it impossible. In May 2026, for example, an FBI investigation into a swatting incident that occurred in Rhode Island in 2024 resulted in the arrest of a 20-year-old suspect in Hungary.

People responsible have been identified and convicted

The best-known case is probably Tyler Barriss.

In December 2017, following a dispute related to Call of Duty, Barriss placed a false call to Wichita police using an address that had been provided to him. He claimed that he had killed his father and was holding his family hostage.

The address was wrong.

Police responded to the home of Andrew Finch, a 28-year-old man who had no connection whatsoever to the dispute. Finch stepped outside without knowing what was happening, and an officer shot and killed him.

Barriss was identified, prosecuted, and ultimately sentenced in 2019 to 20 years in federal prison. He also admitted to dozens of false threats made across the United States. One of the participants who requested the swatting, Casey Viner, was later sentenced to 15 months in prison.

There are much more recent cases. Alan Filion, who was 16–17 years old during much of his criminal activity, carried out more than 375 swatting calls and threats between 2022 and January 2024. He targeted schools, universities, religious institutions, public officials, and private individuals, and even offered swatting as a paid service. In February 2025, he was sentenced to four years in federal prison.

In April 2026, Thomasz Szabo, a Romanian citizen and leader of a group involved in swatting, was sentenced in Washington to 48 months in prison. The group had targeted more than 75 public officials, as well as judges, journalists, and religious institutions.

There have also been particularly unusual cases. Kya Christian Nelson participated in a campaign in which the perpetrators gained access to victims’ Ring cameras, made false emergency calls, and then watched and livestreamed the police response over the Internet. In May 2025, Nelson was sentenced to 44 months in prison.

Four months ago, Trump was branded “𝘢𝘯 𝘰𝘶𝘵𝘳𝘢𝘨𝘦𝘰𝘶𝘴 𝘥𝘪𝘤𝘵𝘢𝘵𝘰𝘳” for pushing to lock down Greenland. This month, he closed a security deal with Denmark giving the U.S. permanent control over the island's defense — while Denmark keeps its sovereignty and Greenlanders keep their right to self-determination on paper.

A guest on a GB News panel didn't hold back on the reversal: “𝘞𝘢𝘴 𝘗𝘳𝘦𝘴𝘪𝘥𝘦𝘯𝘵 𝘛𝘳𝘶𝘮𝘱 𝘳𝘪𝘨𝘩𝘵 𝘢𝘭𝘭 𝘢𝘭𝘰𝘯𝘨? 𝘏𝘦 𝘸𝘢𝘴 𝘤𝘢𝘭𝘭𝘦𝘥 𝘢𝘯 𝘰𝘶𝘵𝘳𝘢𝘨𝘦𝘰𝘶𝘴 𝘥𝘪𝘤𝘵𝘢𝘵𝘰𝘳 𝘢𝘯𝘥 𝘵𝘩𝘳𝘦𝘢𝘵𝘦𝘯𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘸𝘰𝘳𝘭𝘥 𝘰𝘳𝘥𝘦𝘳... 𝘧𝘰𝘶𝘳 𝘮𝘰𝘯𝘵𝘩𝘴 𝘭𝘢𝘵𝘦𝘳, 𝘩𝘦 𝘴𝘦𝘦𝘮𝘴 𝘵𝘰 𝘩𝘢𝘷𝘦 𝘨𝘰𝘵 𝘸𝘩𝘢𝘵 𝘩𝘦 𝘸𝘢𝘯𝘵𝘦𝘥. 𝘐 𝘵𝘩𝘪𝘯𝘬 𝘵𝘩𝘪𝘴 𝘪𝘴 𝘢 𝘨𝘰𝘰𝘥 𝘥𝘦𝘢𝘭.” The terms: 𝐬𝐥𝐨𝐰𝐞𝐫 𝐭𝐞𝐧𝐬𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬 on both sides, and a 𝐬𝐭𝐫𝐨𝐧𝐠𝐞𝐫 𝐜𝐨𝐦𝐦𝐢𝐭𝐦𝐞𝐧𝐭 𝐭𝐨 𝐤𝐞𝐞𝐩𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐂𝐡𝐢𝐧𝐚 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐑𝐮𝐬𝐬𝐢𝐚 𝐨𝐮𝐭 of the Arctic island entirely.

Then came the part that actually stings: back in January, UK Prime Minister Keir Starmer insisted Greenland's future “𝘴𝘩𝘰𝘶𝘭𝘥 𝘣𝘦 𝘥𝘦𝘤𝘪𝘥𝘦𝘥 𝘴𝘰𝘭𝘦𝘭𝘺 𝘣𝘺 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘱𝘦𝘰𝘱𝘭𝘦 𝘰𝘧 𝘎𝘳𝘦𝘦𝘯𝘭𝘢𝘯𝘥 𝘢𝘯𝘥 𝘋𝘦𝘯𝘮𝘢𝘳𝘬.” The panelist's response: “𝘐 𝘩𝘢𝘷𝘦 𝘵𝘰 𝘭𝘢𝘶𝘨𝘩 𝘸𝘩𝘦𝘯 𝘐 𝘴𝘢𝘸 𝘺𝘰𝘶𝘳 𝘷𝘪𝘥𝘦𝘰 𝘰𝘧 𝘚𝘵𝘢𝘳𝘮𝘦𝘳 𝘴𝘢𝘺𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘵𝘩𝘢𝘵 𝘵𝘩𝘪𝘴 𝘪𝘴 𝘶𝘱 𝘵𝘰 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘱𝘦𝘰𝘱𝘭𝘦 𝘰𝘧 𝘎𝘳𝘦𝘦𝘯𝘭𝘢𝘯𝘥 𝘢𝘯𝘥 𝘋𝘦𝘯𝘮𝘢𝘳𝘬, 𝘸𝘩𝘦𝘯 𝘋𝘦𝘯𝘮𝘢𝘳𝘬 𝘸𝘰𝘶𝘭𝘥𝘯'𝘵 𝘭𝘦𝘵 𝘜.𝘚. 𝘰𝘧𝘧𝘪𝘤𝘪𝘢𝘭𝘴 𝘵𝘢𝘭𝘬 𝘵𝘰 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘱𝘦𝘰𝘱𝘭𝘦 𝘰𝘧 𝘎𝘳𝘦𝘦𝘯𝘭𝘢𝘯𝘥.”

In other words: the government insisting Greenlanders alone should decide their fate was, by the panelist's account, the same government that kept Washington from even making its case to them directly — a detail that fits a theory the panelist floated: Copenhagen may have feared what a direct American offer would look like once Greenlanders actually heard it.

Say what you want about how Trump got here. He got a deal that locks two adversaries out of the Arctic, and the loudest critics of his methods can't point to a better outcome they delivered instead.

Honestly wtfk?
Some of the things some of us figured they were doing with the Nvidua acquisition of DGX Lepton never panned out as expected but here is one way of looking at the current situation so not to say you are not correct and my son tells me he observed tge exact same thing as you so...its all interesting. Not trying to be a kniw it all because i know things mostly throughtime in the saddle.

Take this w huge grain if salt. Normally, I run all my serious tech questions through my kids who are both computer science engineers, but nobody has time for that tonight.

My Grok queries tell me this.

IREN is not selling a public “type a prompt, pay per token” API the way Together, Fireworks, or Groq do. It is selling **GPU capacity that clients use to run their own inference**, in two product flavors. That is the whole model.

How they actually sell it

**1. Bare metal clusters (still the core product)**  
The customer gets dedicated NVIDIA boxes — H100, H200, B200, B300, GB300 NVL72 — on IREN’s InfiniBand fabric. No hypervisor in the way. The client installs vLLM, SGLang, TensorRT-LLM, NIM, or whatever they already run, and serves traffic themselves.  
This is what hyperscalers and serious AI labs want: full control, no 15–25% virt tax, predictable latency. Microsoft’s Horizon halls and a large share of the developer deals sit here.

**2. Managed cloud (the layer they are adding)**  
Same GPUs, IREN (now with Mirantis / k0rdent) provisions, orchestrates, monitors, and supports the environment. NVIDIA’s $3.4B contract is explicitly **managed GPU cloud**, not bare metal. That is the template for enterprises and AI-native companies that do not want a platform team. NIM microservices can sit on that stack; IREN markets the clusters as ready for multimodal and reasoning inference, not just training.

There is also a smaller **on-demand** SKU (public list still shows H100 from about $1.99/GPU-hour). That is not where the megawatts are going. Almost all 2026 capacity is multi-year reserved contracts, weighted average term ~4 years, often with customer prepayments covering ~45% of the GPU capex.

Who is already using it for inference-shaped work

Management has said the book now spans **training and inference**, and existing customers are expanding rather than only signing once. Named names that fit inference-heavy products:

- Perplexity (search / serving)
- Fireworks AI and Together AI (they resell inference; they buy IREN wholesale)
- https://t.co/Oqu0Pm1wFJ, Higgsfield (generative media serving)
- Figure AI, Hume (always-on / robotics / interface inference)
- Cohere, an undisclosed frontier lab
- Microsoft and NVIDIA (mixed training + internal serving)

Together and Fireworks renewing is the tell: those firms live on inference APIs. They are parking capacity at IREN, not just training runs.

What the client actually gets for inference

- Same cluster...can train and then serve. IREN’s FAQ is explicit on that.  
- Low-latency fabric (non-blocking 3.2 TB/s InfiniBand) so multi-node serving and long-context / MoE models do not fall over.  
- Mix of air-cooled Blackwell (faster to stand up, good for NVIDIA’s own managed deal) and liquid GB300 NVL72 (dense training *and* high-batch / long-context serving).  
- NVIDIA Exemplar Cloud on B300 and GB300 — useful when a client’s procurement team asks “will NIM / reference recipes actually hit latency and throughput?”  
- Cheap power and no egress fees, which matter more for inference than training because tokens run 24/7.

What they do **not** offer today as a first-class product: a branded IREN inference API, serverless scale-to-zero endpoints, or a Lepton-style marketplace SKU. If a client wants that UX, they bring Fireworks/Together/their own stack and point it at IREN GPUs.

Practical path for a client: [RAN OUT OF SPACE]

text:
TSMC Pushes CoPoS From Round Wafers to Square Panels as AUO, Innolux and Taiwan Suppliers Position for Next-Gen Packaging

September 21, 2026

TSMC has reportedly made several visits to AUO’s facilities in the Central Taiwan Science Park in recent weeks. While the visits are believed to involve discussions over a potential plant acquisition, they may also be tied to TSMC’s broader push into next-generation CoPoS advanced packaging.

As AI chips continue to grow in size, TSMC is working to transition its packaging platform from round wafers to square panels, while also developing glass-core substrate technology.

Supply-chain sources believe AUO’s long-standing expertise in large-format panel manufacturing, glass processing and large-scale factory infrastructure shares some technological common ground with the requirements of panel-level packaging.

One of the key differences between CoPoS and today’s CoWoS architecture is the move away from a round wafer format toward a square panel-based packaging platform.

According to semiconductor industry sources, TSMC’s 3DIC R&D Center in Japan has already begun developing technologies related to glass substrates. Experimental structures reportedly encompass through-glass vias (TGVs), redistribution layers (RDLs), and the integration of components such as GPUs and HBM.

Glass-core substrates offer potential advantages in physical characteristics such as coplanarity, coefficient of thermal expansion (CTE) and stiffness, making glass an increasingly attractive option as TSMC looks to scale CoPoS to larger package sizes.

TGV Emerges as a Key Battleground

On the process side, TGV formation is expected to become one of the main areas of competition across the supply chain.

The approach currently drawing the most attention combines ultrafast laser processing with wet etching.

In this process, picosecond or femtosecond lasers are first used to modify the glass, after which chemical etching creates the via holes. The technique can reduce the thermal stress and microcracking associated with conventional laser drilling.

Once the TGVs are formed, the substrate must still undergo a series of additional process steps, including cleaning, copper plating, chemical mechanical planarization (CMP) and RDL formation.

As the number of RDL layers continues to rise, demand for related equipment, chemicals and materials is also expected to increase.

Inspection Could Be One of the Biggest Challenges in CoPoS Mass Production

Inspection is expected to be one of the most critical hurdles in bringing CoPoS into volume production.

Industry sources note that microcracks can form in glass after laser drilling, copper plating and thermal processing. Once formed, those cracks can propagate toward neighboring TGVs, potentially degrading electrical performance and downstream packaging yields.

As a result, suppliers are deploying a range of inspection technologies, including automated optical inspection (AOI), 3D near-infrared imaging (3D NIR) and X-ray inspection.

Internal microcracks that develop after copper plating are particularly difficult to detect using conventional optical inspection because light cannot easily penetrate the structure. X-ray inspection is therefore emerging as an important solution for detecting such hidden defects.

Taiwan’s Supply Chain Moves Early to Secure a Position

Taiwanese suppliers are also moving early to secure positions in the emerging CoPoS ecosystem.

In glass processing and laser-related equipment, the market is currently focusing on companies including Innolux (群創), Contrel Technology (東捷) and E&R Engineering (鈦昇).

For wet processing, cleaning and metallization equipment, potential suppliers include Scientech (辛耘) and Grand Process Technology (弘塑).

Companies positioned in downstream thermal processing and factory automation include All Ring Tech (萬潤), C Sun Manufacturing (志聖), AblePrint Technology (印能科技) and Gallant Precision Machining (群翊).

Meanwhile, as detecting microcracks inside glass becomes increasingly challenging, companies specializing in metrology, inspection and failure analysis — including Machvision (牧德), Favite (晶彩科), Chroma ATE (致茂), Ta Liang Technology (大量) and iST (宜特) — could also find opportunities to enter the CoPoS supply chain.

text:
Key quotes from the official 60 Minutes transcript, grouped by theme. Source: CBS News transcript.

On Lindsay’s decline

“No. I could piece together what it was like to be really, really anxious or depressed, but I didn’t know how to manage a postpartum illness. I think mental illness has this ability to be tragically deceptive. So I’m sure there are things that I didn’t see.”

“December was a big struggle for her—just a huge lack of sleep, deep, deep depression, intrusive thoughts, and at the end of that month she went to the hospital.”

On Callan

“I really thought there was a chance that Callan would live. And I remember just thinking, ‘Just gimme one. Just gimme one kid, and I would raise him as best I could, and I would give him the best life I possibly could. I’d tell him about his brother and sister.’”

“I’m so grateful for those four days that I had with him. And I’m so grateful he hung on.”

“I said, ‘I’m so sorry.’ And I got to hold him. I got to lay down next to him. And he died in my arms.”

On forgiveness

“I saw headlines that said, you know, ‘Killer Mom,’ and ‘Baby Murderer,’ ‘Monster.’ And none of ’em were accurate. I believe that it was her mental illness that caused that. … When it comes to forgiveness, I also felt that if I didn’t get there, I would be eaten up inside forever.”

Asked if Lindsay ever asked for forgiveness: “No. But I gave it to her.”

On whether she remembered the killings: “She said it was like a dream. And she remembered it much in the way you would remember a dream after waking up.”

On guilt and grief

“I think I did the best I could with what I had at the time. And I live with the outcome. I live with it every day.”

“There was a time where I didn’t think I would live to see my 35th birthday. And I was completely fine with it.”

On Callan’s first birthday after the deaths: “I go to St. Patrick’s Cathedral. I light a candle, and I say, ‘I love you, buddy.’ And I walk out on Fifth Avenue and I start crying my eyes out. And nobody cared. … I thought, ‘This is where I need to be. I can grieve.’”

text:
The Kathy Hochul Debacle
How One Person Can Run a State Into the Ground
Daily Countdown to November 3rd — Day 8 — 44 Days Until Election Day — September 20, 2026
A structural deficit is what you have when recurring spending outruns recurring revenue, year after year, regardless of how any single year closes out. A bad year is an accident. What follows is not a bad-year story. It is a decision story, repeated.
Why One Person's Name Belongs on This
New York runs on what's called a strong executive budget system. Article VII of the state Constitution gives the governor, not the Legislature, the power to write the budget the Legislature then votes on. The Legislature can reduce or strike the governor's appropriations, but it cannot add new items to the governor's bills — it can only add money through separate bills the governor must sign or veto. That structure is exactly why a governor's name carries more weight on a state budget than any single legislator's ever could. The framers built it that way on purpose, according to constitutional historians, because they judged the Legislature chronically averse to accountability and prone to fiscal irresponsibility. A system built to concentrate responsibility in one office is a system where that officeholder doesn't get to share the blame when the numbers go bad.
The Legislature does negotiate, amend, and add cost during the process — this piece will get to that. But the executive budget system means the frame, the base numbers, and the public announcement of what was agreed to are the governor's product first.
The Number She Announced
On May 7, 2026, the governor's office announced a budget agreement of approximately $268 billion. When the state's own Financial Plan was released on June 10, weeks later, it put the real, enacted total at $277.0 billion — $9.0 billion, or 3.4 percent, higher than what had just been announced to the public.
That $277.0 billion is a 7.0 percent increase, $18.1 billion, over last year's budget. All Funds revenue is projected at $269.8 billion, an increase of only 1.1 percent, or $2.8 billion. By simple subtraction of the state's own projections, spending exceeds revenue by roughly $7.2 billion in this year alone.
The budget is still legally called "balanced." That's possible because the constitutional and statutory test is narrow: only the General Fund has to balance, and only on a cash basis — money counted when it moves, not when it's earned or owed. Neither the state Constitution nor the State Finance Law defines "balance" with any precision. Even under that loose test, the plan draws down $1.3 billion of General Fund balance to get there. On a GAAP accrual basis — the accounting standard a real business or a household budget review would actually use — New York's own financial plans have shown deficits even in years the cash-basis version was called "balanced." The most recent all-funds GAAP figure independently confirmed for this piece was a $2.1 billion operating deficit as of 2019-20; a current-year GAAP figure was not available and should not be assumed to match today's number.
A $9 billion gap between the number announced to the public and the number in the actual enacted plan is either sloppy accounting or careful sequencing — announce the smaller number when cameras are rolling, let the real number land in a report weeks later. The documentary record shows the gap. It does not show intent, and this piece does not claim to know what was in anyone's head. What it will not do is pretend the gap isn't there.
What the Numbers Say Happens Next
The state's own Division of the Budget projects disbursements exceeding receipts in every single year of the four-year Financial Plan — not a one-year dip, a sustained pattern. The cumulative General Fund budget gap for fiscal years 2028 through 2030 is $31.7 billion: $6.4 billion in FY28, $10.5 billion in FY29, and $14.7 billion in FY30. That three-year cumulative gap equals 7.4 percent of the $428.4 billion the state itself projects it will spend from the General Fund over that span.
General Fund spending is projected to grow 17.7 percent from FY27 to FY30. General Fund receipts over the same period are projected to grow 4.9 percent. A nearly four-to-one gap between spending growth and revenue growth, sustained across a four-year projection the state's own budget office produced, is not noise. It is a structural imbalance, and calling it anything softer understates what the state's own numbers say.
The gap actually got worse between January and June of this year — up roughly $4.1 billion — after negotiated changes during the legislative session added about $9.2 billion in new General Fund costs, only partly offset by about $5.4 billion in favorable revisions elsewhere. Of the $4.1 billion in new spending added in the final negotiation, $1.44 billion was classified as recurring — meaning it doesn't go away next year — while $1.27 billion was labeled "non-recurring." The Comptroller's office notes, by name, that several items repeatedly labeled "one-time" in past budgets — including $500 million a year for distressed hospitals, now in its fourth consecutive year — keep reappearing. A "one-time" cost that shows up four years running isn't one-time. It's recurring spending wearing a label that makes the budget look better than it is.
Reserves — the rainy-day cushion meant to absorb a downturn — are remaining flat at approximately $15.1 billion even as the underlying budget keeps growing. Total reserves reached a record $21.6 billion in SFY 2024, representing 16.2 percent of State Operating Funds spending at the time. Since then, largely because the state used $6.5 billion in available resources to repay a federal unemployment insurance loan, the informal "Economic Uncertainties" reserve component has dropped, and reserves as a share of the budget have declined and are projected to keep declining, even as the statutory rainy-day funds themselves grow to a nominal record. A reserve fund that stays flat in dollars while the budget grows around it is shrinking in every way that matters — as a percentage, and as a cushion against the next recession.
The Debt Underneath
Over the past five fiscal years, New York has prepaid approximately $25.6 billion in debt service — including $4.5 billion last year alone — and the current plan assumes $1.5 billion more will be prepaid this year. The state's own Comptroller says these prepayments, while producing some modest interest savings, function to mask the growing trajectory of debt service costs and distort year-over-year comparisons of revenue and spending growth. Adjusted to strip out the effect of prepayments, baseline debt service costs are projected to rise nearly 44 percent between SFY 2026 and SFY 2031 — from $6.415 billion to $9.232 billion.
Total state-supported debt outstanding is projected to grow from $60.3 billion to $98.8 billion over the next five years — an increase of roughly 64 percent. Nearly all of that increase comes from what's called "backdoor borrowing" — debt issued by public authorities that the state is contractually obligated to repay but that never went before voters, which the Constitution otherwise requires for state debt. More than 51 percent of all capital spending in the current five-year plan is projected to come from this backdoor debt, versus roughly 2 percent from voter-approved general obligation bonds. As this debt grows, the room remaining under the state's own statutory debt cap shrinks to just $177 million by SFY 2031 — a razor-thin margin for a state spending nearly $300 billion a year.
The state's SFY 2025 audited financial report showed $62.2 billion in total debt outstanding and a $60.6 billion net liability for retiree health benefits (OPEB) — obligations promised to public employees that are not yet funded.
Where New York Stacks Up Against the Other 49
On raw dollars, New York carries the second-highest total state government debt in the nation, behind only California — roughly $233 billion by one comprehensive measure, versus California's $497 billion. By Moody's narrower net tax-supported debt measure, New York again ranks second in the nation in dollar terms, at $67.6 billion, behind only California.
Per resident, New York's debt burden ranks seventh-highest in the nation under Moody's measure, at roughly $3,453 per person against a 50-state median of $1,189. As a share of personal income, New York's net tax-supported debt ranks tenth-highest, at 4.2 percent versus a median of 2.2 percent. As a share of state GDP, New York ranks thirteenth, at 3.4 percent versus a median of 2.0 percent. On long-term debt specifically, one broader measure put New York twelfth among all states in per-capita terms, at $7,615 per resident — well behind the very worst states (Connecticut near $26,000, New Jersey near $23,000) but still comfortably in the most-indebted tier, not the middle of the pack and nowhere near the best-managed states.
New York is not the single worst-indebted state in America. It does not need to be for this to be a genuine crisis. Being the second-largest debtor in absolute dollars, inside the top ten to fifteen states on every per-capita and income-relative measure, and trending toward record debt levels over the next five years, is bad enough on its own. A governor doesn't get credit for "we're not Connecticut."
The Process Behind the Numbers
The SFY 2027 budget was not enacted until May 27, 2026 — 57 days after the April 1 start of the fiscal year, and the latest budget in the Comptroller's records going back to SFY 2017, which began a run of increasingly late budgets: 32 days late in 2024, 20 days late in 2025, 38 days late in 2026, and now 57 in 2027. Despite the extended process, several of the budget bills were passed using "messages of necessity" — a legislative mechanism that waives the normal three-day waiting period between a bill's introduction and a floor vote, on the stated grounds that immediate action is necessary. Two of the largest bills, covering education and public protection spending, were passed this way even though voting on other budget bills continued for another week afterward — meaning the emergency justification for skipping public review didn't match how the rest of the process actually unfolded. When a budget takes 57 days to negotiate but the individual bills still get rushed past the public with an emergency waiver, that combination should raise more questions than it typically gets asked.
The enacted budget exempts approximately $1.5 billion in state spending from the Comptroller's independent oversight and from competitive bidding requirements outright, and permits an additional $3 billion to be spent without competitive bidding under related provisions. The changes also raise discretionary purchasing thresholds to $150,000 for most state agencies, SUNY, and CUNY, and raise the threshold for OSC's own contract-approval authority to the same figure. In 2025 alone, nearly 6,000 contracts fell in the $50,000-to-$300,000 range that these threshold increases now push outside independent review — representing close to $1 billion. A budget that grows faster than revenue, gets finalized later every year, and simultaneously narrows the state's own watchdog's authority over how the money is spent is not a coincidence of circumstances. It is a pattern, and patterns are choices.

Where the Money Is Actually Going
The two largest drivers of state spending growth are Medicaid and School Aid — together known in Albany budget circles as "the Big Two." In SFY 2019, Medicaid across all state agencies totaled about $20.7 billion, or 20.7 percent of State Operating Funds spending; by SFY 2026 it had grown to roughly $39.4 billion, or 26.5 percent. The state's own projections show it reaching $53.3 billion by SFY 2030 — 29 percent of the budget. School Aid, even after the state's Foundation Aid formula was declared "fully funded," still grew to just over $37 billion in SFY 2026 and is projected to reach $43.7 billion by SFY 2030. Combined, Medicaid and School Aid are projected to consume 52.8 percent of State Operating Funds spending by SFY 2030, up from 46.9 percent in SFY 2019.
State-share Medicaid spending alone is projected to grow $5 billion, or 11.7 percent, in this budget year, driven by minimum-wage increases for health care workers, rising medical and drug costs, and continued growth in aging and high-utilization populations. The state projects Medicaid will exceed its own "Global Cap" — the mechanism created specifically to constrain Medicaid cost growth — by $430 million in FY28, growing to a $3.2 billion overage by FY30, as costs shift from the expiring Essential Plan onto Medicaid. The share of Medicaid spending exempted from that cap altogether has grown from about 4 percent when the cap was created to an estimated 25 percent today. A spending cap that exempts a quarter of the spending it's supposed to cap, and is on track to be breached anyway within two years, is not functioning as a cap. It is functioning as a talking point.
The Essential Plan Cliff
The Essential Plan covered approximately 1.8 million New Yorkers in SFY 2026, including lawfully present immigrants who don't qualify for federally financed Medicaid because of their immigration status. The 2025 federal budget law, P.L. 119-21, cut off premium tax credits for many of those enrollees starting January 1, 2026, and eliminates federal funding for Essential Plan benefits for certain lawfully present immigrants starting January 1, 2027.
In response, the state received federal approval to terminate the Essential Plan's existing waiver and reactivate a dormant "Basic Health Plan" program effective July 1, 2026. Roughly 1.4 million current enrollees with incomes below 200 percent of the federal poverty level will keep coverage under that shift. But approximately 450,000 New Yorkers with incomes between 200 and 250 percent of the poverty line will lose Essential Plan eligibility entirely, left to find coverage through the state's insurance marketplace, an employer plan, or go without. The state estimates its own available resources are sufficient to fund the replacement Basic Health Plan only through December 31, 2028 — after that, funding is undetermined. Essential Plan receipts are projected to fall from $14.6 billion in SFY 2026 to $9.1 billion in SFY 2027, and below $7 billion in SFY 2028 and SFY 2029, with the state's own budget office listing SFY 2030 simply as "to be determined." State-only costs to cover the population losing federal support are estimated at nearly $7 billion through SFY 2028.
A related mechanism, the Healthcare Stability Fund, is funded by an assessment on Managed Care Organizations that the federal government approved effective January 2025. A 2025 federal draft rule and P.L. 119-21 both introduced new conditions the existing assessment doesn't meet, and while a January 2026 federal rule lets New York keep collecting through the end of this year, the state's replacement assessment beginning January 2027 is expected to generate only $165 million annually — a fraction of the roughly $5.5 billion the original assessment brought in across SFY 2026 and SFY 2027 combined. The fund is projected to disburse $4.1 billion this year to hospitals, nursing homes, and safety-net providers, then fall toward zero by SFY 2030 as the replacement revenue comes in far short. Federal law now also prohibits new provider taxes and restricts increases to existing ones, leaving the General Fund as the only clear backstop once the Healthcare Stability Fund runs dry.
The School Aid Formula Fight
Total School Aid spending is projected at $39.1 billion this year, a $2.0 billion, 5.4 percent increase. School Aid growth is technically capped by a formula tied to state personal income growth, but the state's own budget office says School Aid increases have exceeded that cap almost every year since it was created in SFY 2012. For the second year running, this budget rewrites pieces of the underlying Foundation Aid formula — adding new weighting for homeless children and foster youth, and increasing the weighting for English Language Learners — while also guaranteeing every school district a minimum 2 percent increase regardless of enrollment or need. The budget further expands universal prekindergarten, raising per-pupil funding to the higher of $10,000 or a district's Foundation Aid per-pupil rate, and requires every district to offer pre-K by the 2028-29 school year. New York City alone is set to receive $205 million for its separate "3-K" program.
A funding cap that gets exceeded almost every year isn't a cap. It's a floor with a label on it.
Solutions — From the People Whose Job Is to Audit This, Not Attack It
The state Comptroller's own recommendations, made repeatedly in official reports rather than campaign messaging, include: matching any new recurring spending with recurring revenue rather than one-time resources; growing reserves to keep pace with the growth of the overall budget rather than letting them go flat; establishing comprehensive, binding constitutional debt limits rather than the current statutory cap that the Legislature can and does adjust; and prioritizing long-term debt reduction over the short-term political benefit of annual debt-service prepayments. The nonpartisan Citizens Budget Commission has separately called for the state to budget and report using modified-accrual GAAP accounting rather than cash accounting, precisely so that timing shifts and prepayments can no longer be used to make a budget look more balanced on paper than it is in practice.
None of these recommendations come from a political opponent. They come from the state's own independent fiscal watchdog and a nonpartisan budget-research organization that has praised this same governor by name when the record warranted it.
What Is at Stake on November 3rd
If the state's own projections hold and no corrective action is taken, whoever occupies the governor's office starting in January inherits budget gaps of $6.4 billion, $10.5 billion, and $14.7 billion in the three years that follow — with a reserve fund that is a shrinking share of an ever-larger budget, and a debt ceiling with only $177 million of room left under it by 2031. New York elects a governor to a four-year term, and 2026 is a gubernatorial election year.
None of the numbers above required an adjective to make the case. The gap between what was announced and what was enacted, the four-to-one ratio of spending growth to revenue growth, the debt approaching its legal ceiling, and the watchdog's own oversight being narrowed in the same budget that grew the fastest — these facts carry their own weight. Whether one person should be held to account for a structure that concentrates this much authority in one office is not a numbers question. It's the question this series exists to keep asking every day between now and November 3rd.
When a governor's own independent Comptroller — not a rival party, her own state's fiscal watchdog — lays out this pattern in an official report, what's left of the defense that this is just partisan noise?
The Choice on November 3rd
Before becoming governor, Kathy Hochul had never held a chief-executive office. Her path ran from Erie County Clerk to Congress to Lieutenant Governor — a position with no independent executive authority under the state Constitution — before she ascended to Governor in August 2021 when Andrew Cuomo resigned. She was never elected to a chief-executive post first; she inherited one. Bruce Blakeman, the Republican and Conservative Party nominee she now faces, has run Nassau County's government directly as County Executive since 2022. On November 3rd, New York voters choose between a governor who inherited the state's top executive job and a challenger who has already run one. Time for a change.

text:
HOW THE OPERATION WORKS
The criminal structure is sophisticated and hierarchical. Specialized "builders" construct skimming devices so well-made that even diligent merchants miss them . Lower-level members install them at gas stations, convenience stores, and grocery markets, often using accomplices to distract cashiers . Some devices have Bluetooth transmitters, allowing data to be downloaded remotely . The stolen card numbers are then loaded onto cloned cards—often blank plastic or old gift cards—and used to withdraw cash at ATMs or make bulk purchases . In just over a week, one Cleveland-based crew stole 981 food stamp accounts, sometimes selling the stolen card data for $2,500 each .
THE HUMAN COST
The victims are among America's most vulnerable. "These criminals target people living one paycheck away from crisis," said U.S. Attorney Adam Gordon. "Exploiting that vulnerability is as cruel as it is criminal" . When benefits are drained, families are left without money for food until the next monthly allocation. The problem became so severe that Congress temporarily allowed the USDA to reimburse victims, but that mechanism was eliminated—meaning affected households often receive nothing . As one Ohio legislator who sponsored a chip-card bill put it: there is "a special place in hell for those who steal from the poor" .

THE MONEY TRAIL
The illicit proceeds fund lifestyles far removed from the victims. Authorities describe rented luxury cars, homes with infinity pools, and cryptocurrency transfers back to Romania that flow into real estate, gambling, and crime bosses . In one case, Romanian authorities seized a house in Transylvania belonging to a man convicted of money laundering . A joint Romanian-Italian operation recently captured three brothers who led a network operating across Romania, Italy, Austria, and the United States, hiding one of them behind a false wall in Italy .
THE PATH FORWARD
California's experience offers a template. After adopting chip-and-tap EBT cards, the state reported an 83% drop in overall EBT theft between January 2024 and November 2025 . Ohio's House passed a bill 90-0 to require chip-enabled SNAP cards, with $5.3 million in state funding . But most states lag behind, and investigators warn the problem will persist as long as benefits can be accessed through magnetic stripes alone . For now, Romanian organized crime groups continue to treat America's welfare system as an ATM—and the poorest Americans pay the price.

text:
“The lack of relegation for a head coach making his first step, it leads you to get a little bit more time if you are flirting at the bottom of the league. There's not so much panic.”

Former Tottenham Hotspur assistant Matt Wells explains why he chose to coach Colorado Rapids.

He spoke to CBS Sports recently, and was asked why he came to MLS to begin his head coaching career instead of staying in England.

Wells helped Tottenham win the Europa League as an assistant. He also had stints at Fulham, Bournemouth, and Club Brugge.

“I had a wonderful journey at Tottenham, and I really felt like the lift,” he said.

“I'm a Tottenham fan as well, of course, which is well documented with my granddad playing in the '60s.

“To be the assistant manager when I went back there, my desperation was to lift a trophy and help the club lift a trophy. 

“So to do that with the Europa League, it felt like a good time to depart. I've always had ambitions to be a head coach. I felt ready for a number of years, but I sort of always found a reason to stay. 

“And when Ange made me assistant, it was such a great privilege and honor to do that at Tottenham. I sort of parked my own ambitions at that time and stayed. 

“And once we lifted the trophy, it was the right time to move. Then you just have to be strategic: where's the right place to go and make your first steps? 

“And I had a couple of offers in the Championship, and I just felt in discussions with those clubs, it was just very short-term. 

“Because it was December, it was like these teams that I was talking to were generally lower in the table. 

“Of course in England, there's the threat of relegation. So I could feel the tension and the stress and the pressure from the hierarchy at those clubs that we just have to win on Saturday by hook or by crook. 

“And it's not something that really appealed to me, whereas at the same time, having discussions with the guys at Colorado, it was very much about transformation. 

“It was, ‘Okay, we've missed out on the playoffs. We don't necessarily have a playing style. We want something that people can just look at us and they know that's the Colorado Rapids. Can you come in and build something long-term over a number of years, shape the team in your image? We'll give you the keys to the kingdom in terms of recruitment.’

“Of course it's within constraints. I knew coming into it. I looked at the numbers, we're 27th in budget out of 30 teams, but I'm a coach, so those things don't deter me. I wanted to come here and create something special. 

“It's got great ownership here, guys that really want to do something special. They want to create a team that the fans are proud of, and so it was a much more exciting pitch for me. 

“And I guess looking also strategically at the league and the lack of relegation for a head coach making his first step, the lack of relegation does also tend to lead you  to get a little bit more time if you are flirting at the bottom of the league. 

“There's not so much panic if guys can see you're a good coach and you're building something special, then they're willing to be a bit more patient. 

“So all those things factored in, it seemed like a great move, and then the key was once my wife gave it the green light that she was willing to move to America, I did have to buy her a handbag just to sweeten the deal, but we convinced her, and now we're here and we love it over here. 

“We're having a great time. My wife's happy, my daughter's really happy, and certainly professionally I'm very happy. So yeah, long may it continue.”

Rapids are currently in the playoff spot, being ranked seventh in the Western Conference.
